title: Attention Is All You Need
abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.

sections.text: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. sections.name: Introduction
sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recurrent neural networks, especially long short-term memory and gated recurrent neural networks, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling. Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output.

sections.name: Methodology
sections.heading: 3 Model Architecture
sections.text: The Transformer follows this overall architecture using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder. The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

sections.name: Results & Discussion
sections.heading: 5 Results
sections.text: On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, the big transformer model outperforms the best previously reported models by more than 2.0 BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our big model achieves a BLEU score of 41.8, outperforming all previously reported single models, at 1/4 the training cost of the previous state-of-the-art model.

sections.name: Limitations
sections.heading: 6 Limitations & Complexity
sections.text: While self-attention connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, its computational complexity per layer is O(n^2 * d), where n is the sequence length and d is the representation dimension. When the sequence length n is very large, self-attention layers can become computationally and memory prohibitive compared to restricted recurrent layers.

summary.title: Attention Is All You Need
summary.executiveSummary: Prior to this work, sequence transduction was dominated by recurrent neural networks (RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs) and convolutional architectures. While effective, recurrent models process sequences token-by-token in a sequential fashion, which prevents parallelization during training and leads to memory and gradient degradation over long sequences. This landmark paper introduces the Transformer, the first sequence transduction model relying entirely on self-attention mechanisms to model global dependencies between input and output representations without any recurrence or convolution. The Transformer trains significantly faster than recurrent baselines and achieves superior translation quality on international benchmarks.
coreContributions: Elimination of Recurrent Inductive Biases: Replaces sequential recurrent hidden states with parallelized Multi-Head Scaled Dot-Product Attention, allowing all token interactions across a sequence to be computed simultaneously.

Scaled Dot-Product Attention Mechanism: Introduces the scaling factor 1 / sqrt(d_k) in the denominator of the dot product quotient inside the softmax function, mathematically counteracting gradient vanishing in dot products of high dimensionality.

Multi-Head Representation Subspaces: Projects queries, keys, and values across h=8 independent linear subspaces, enabling the network to jointly attend to syntactic, positional, and semantic relationships at different positions.

Sinusoidal Positional Encoding: Formulates continuous trigonometric wavelength functions that inject sequential order into the permutation-invariant self-attention matrices without adding learnable recurrent parameters.

State-of-the-Art Translation & Training Efficiency: Established SOTA BLEU scores of 28.4 on WMT 2014 English-to-German and 41.8 on English-to-French while requiring only 3.5 days of training on 8 P100 GPUs (a fraction of prior models).

methodology.architecture: The architecture employs an Encoder-Decoder structure consisting of N = 6 stacked identical layers for both encoder and decoder. Each encoder layer contains two sub-layers: (1) a multi-head self-attention module and (2) a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network (FFN with inner dimension d_ff = 2048 and model dimension d_model = 512). A residual connection surrounds each sub-layer, followed by Layer Normalization: Output = LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The decoder adds a third sub-layer that performs multi-head attention over the encoder output representations, while employing causal masking to prevent positions from attending to future tokens during auto-regressive generation.
keyTechniques: Scaled Dot-Product Attention: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( (Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k) ) * V, where sqrt(d_k) divides the dot product to scale down large values and preserve gradient flow.

Multi-Head Attention: MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_h) * W_O, where each head_i = Attention(Q * W_i^Q, K * W_i^K, V * W_i^V) projects representations into d_k = d_model / h = 64 dimensions.
Sinusoidal Positional Embeddings: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i / d_model)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i / d_model)), allowing the model to extrapolate to arbitrary sequence lengths.
Residual Connections & Pre-LN: Stabilizes gradient propagation through 12 total attention and feed-forward layers.
benchmarksUsed: WMT 2014 English-to-German (4.5 million sentence pairs, evaluated with standard tokenized BLEU)
WMT 2014 English-to-French (36 million sentence pairs, evaluated with standard tokenized BLEU)
English Constituency Parsing (Penn Treebank WSJ section 23, evaluated with F1 score)
methodology.mathematicalFormulation:
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( (Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k) ) * V

Where:
• Q (Query matrix) represents current token lookup states [n x d_k]
• K (Key matrix) represents indexed token states [m x d_k]
• V (Value matrix) holds actual semantic representations to be aggregated [m x d_v]
• d_k is the key dimensionality (64 in the base model). In the dot-product quotient inside softmax, dividing by sqrt(d_k) prevents the dot products from growing excessively large for large dimensions, which would otherwise push softmax into saturated regions with vanishingly small gradients.

quantitativeResults: WMT 2014 English-to-German: Base model scored 27.3 BLEU; Big model achieved 28.4 BLEU, establishing a new SOTA by over 2.0 BLEU points above all prior single and ensemble models.
WMT 2014 English-to-French: Big model achieved 41.8 BLEU, outperforming previously published single models while training for only 3.5 days at 1/4 the compute cost of competing models.
Constituency Parsing: Generalization to English constituency parsing achieved an F1 of 91.3 with little task-specific tuning, outperforming all prior models except RNN grammars.
Training Wall-Clock Speed: Base model trained in 12 hours on 8 P100 GPUs; Big model trained in 3.5 days (2.3 x 10^19 FLOPs vs 1.0 x 10^20 for GNMT+RL baselines).
qualitativeInsights: Analysis of individual attention heads revealed that different heads learn specialized linguistic functions: some heads attend to long-range pronominal reference (e.g. matching "it" across 15 words to its antecedent noun), while others capture verb-argument structures and clause boundaries.
The attention distribution forms interpretable alignment graphs that clearly show cross-lingual token reordering.

limitations: Quadratic Computational & Memory Complexity: Self-attention scales as Complexity = O(n^2 * d) with respect to input sequence length n. For long documents (n > 4096), memory consumption for storing the n x n attention matrix becomes prohibitive without specialized sparse kernels.

Lack of Inductive Bias for Locality: Unlike CNNs which naturally enforce local spatial invariance, the Transformer must learn locality purely through data, necessitating large pre-training datasets to prevent overfitting on small tasks.

Autoregressive Inference Latency: While training is fully parallelized across all tokens, inference remains sequential (generating one token at a time), requiring key-value (KV) caching to avoid recomputing past representations.
practicalImplications: Foundation of all modern Large Language Models: Directly catalyzed GPT-1/2/3/4, BERT, T5, Gemini, Claude, LLaMA, and modern multimodal diffusion architectures.
Hardware Utilization: Highly dense matrix multiplications (GEMM) match modern GPU/TPU tensor core architectures, maximizing hardware FLOPS utilization compared to memory-bound RNN hidden states.

keyEquationsOrTheorems.formulaOrDescription: PE(pos, 2i) = sin( pos / 10000^(2i / d_model) ), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 10000^(2i / d_model) )

strengths: Flawless parallelization of training sequences across GPU tensor cores.
Direct connection between any pair of sequence positions with path length O(1), preventing vanishing gradients.
Exceptionally clean, modular architecture that scales predictably with parameters and compute.
weaknesses: Quadratic memory bottleneck on long sequence lengths was unaddressed in the original paper.
Requires careful learning rate warmup schedules and label smoothing to stabilize training convergence.
potentialBiases: Evaluated primarily on high-resource Indo-European language pairs (English, German, French) where large parallel corpora were readily available.

title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
abstract: An important paradigm of natural language processing consists of large-scale pre-training on general domain data and adaptation to particular tasks. As we pre-train larger models, full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible. We propose Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, which freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks.

As we pre-train larger models, full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible. We propose Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, which freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks.

sections.name: Methodology
sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: A neural network contains many dense layers which perform matrix multiplication. The weight matrices in these layers typically have full-rank. When adapting to a specific task, Aghajanyan et al. (2020) shows that the pre-trained language models have a low "intrinsic dimension". Inspired by this, we hypothesize the updates to the weights also have a low "intrinsic rank" during adaptation. For a pre-trained weight matrix W0 in R^(d x k), we constrain its update by representing the latter with a low-rank decomposition W0 + Delta W = W0 + BA, where B in R^(d x r), A in R^(r x k), and the rank r << min(d, k).

summary.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
summary.executiveSummary: Full parameter fine-tuning of multi-billion parameter foundation models (such as GPT-3 175B) is computationally intractable for individual tasks, requiring hundreds of gigabytes of optimizer states and independent model checkpoints for each specialized downstream domain. This work proposes Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which freezes the pre-trained model weights W_0 and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices (A and B) into each attention layer of the Transformer. By hypothesizing and verifying that weight updates during downstream adaptation have a very low intrinsic rank, LoRA reduces trainable parameters by up to 10,000 times and GPU memory consumption by 3 times, while introducing zero additional inference latency when merged back into the frozen base model weights.
coreContributions: Low-Rank Parameterization Hypothesis: Formulates weight updates Delta W as the product of two low-rank matrices B and A (where rank r << min(d, k)), demonstrating that downstream task adaptations occupy a manifold of extremely low intrinsic dimension.

Zero Inference Latency Overhead: Because W = W_0 + (alpha / r) * B * A, the adapted weights can be linearly added directly into the pre-trained weights W_0 upon deployment, creating zero additional architectural latency or inference compute overhead.

Dramatic Memory & Storage Reduction: Decreases required fine-tuning VRAM from 1.2 Terabytes down to 350 Gigabytes for GPT-3 175B, and slashes per-task checkpoint sizes from 350GB to under 35MB (a 10,000x storage savings).
Modular Multi-Tenant Model Serving: Enables hosting a single frozen 175B foundation model in GPU memory and hot-swapping lightweight task adapters in milliseconds based on user routing.

methodology.architecture: LoRA freezes the pre-trained weight matrix W_0 in R^(d x k) across chosen Transformer linear layers (predominantly the attention projection matrices W_q and W_v). It introduces a parallel adapter branch consisting of two matrix multiplications: matrix A in R^(r x k) initialized with random Gaussian noise N(0, sigma^2), and matrix B in R^(d x r) initialized strictly to zero. Consequently, at the beginning of training, the product Delta W = B * A evaluates exactly to zero, guaranteeing that the pre-trained model behavior is unchanged at initialization. The forward pass is computed as h = W_0 * x + (alpha / r) * B * A * x, where alpha is a constant scaling hyperparameter.
keyTechniques: Weight Factorization: W = W_0 + (alpha / r) * B * A, where r is typically chosen between 4 and 16.
Zero Initialization of Matrix B: Ensures training starts exactly from the pre-trained model state without disruption.
Constant Scaling Factor (alpha / r): Stabilizes gradient updates when adjusting the rank r, avoiding the need to retune learning rates.
Targeted Module Injection: Demonstrates that adapting attention projection weights (W_q, W_v) is more parameter-efficient than adapting feed-forward layers or all weight matrices.
benchmarksUsed: GLUE Benchmark (MNLI, SST-2, MRPC, CoLA, QNLI, QQP, RTE, STS-B) with RoBERTa-large and DeBERTa-XXL
WikiSQL and SAMSum conversational abstractive summarization with GPT-2 and GPT-3 175B
E2E NLG Challenge evaluated across BLEU, NIST, METEOR, ROUGE-L, and CIDEr metrics
methodology.mathematicalFormulation:
h = W_0 * x + Delta W * x = W_0 * x + (alpha / r) * B * A * x

Where:
• W_0 is the frozen pre-trained weight matrix [d x k]
• x is the input representation vector [k x 1]
• B is the up-projection trainable matrix [d x r], initialized to 0
• A is the down-projection trainable matrix [r x k], initialized with Gaussian N(0, sigma^2)
• r is the intrinsic rank constraint (r << min(d, k), e.g. r = 4, 8, 16)
• alpha is a constant scaling factor (e.g. alpha = 16 or 32)

quantitativeResults: GPT-3 175B Performance: LoRA achieves 73.4% accuracy on WikiSQL (matching full fine-tuning at 73.8%) while training only 37.7 million parameters compared to 175 billion.
RoBERTa and DeBERTa: Matches or outperforms full fine-tuning across all GLUE benchmark tasks with a fraction of trainable parameters (0.01% of model weights).
Memory Footprint: Slashes VRAM consumption during training by 3x (from 1.2TB to 350GB), enabling GPT-3 175B fine-tuning without model checkpoint partitioning across nodes.
Storage Savings: Adapter checkpoints are under 35MB, allowing researchers to store 10,000 custom domain models in the disk space previously needed for a single fine-tuned model.
qualitativeInsights: Subspace Similarity Analysis (Grassmannian distance): Empirical investigation shows that low-rank adaptation matrices A and B correlate strongly with the top singular vectors of full fine-tuning weight updates, confirming that downstream learning primarily occurs in an extremely low-dimensional subspace.
Rank Generalization: Increasing rank r beyond 8 yielded minimal accuracy gains for standard classification and generation benchmarks, supporting the low intrinsic dimension hypothesis.

limitations: Multi-Task Batching Overhead: If multiple distinct tasks must be evaluated concurrently within the same mini-batch, one cannot simply merge W = W_0 + B*A into the weights; instead, dynamic kernel dispatching is required to apply different adapters per sample.

Domain Knowledge Memorization: LoRA excels at style, format, and task adaptation, but may underperform full fine-tuning on domain adaptation tasks requiring extensive new factual knowledge memorization (such as continuous pre-training on medical textbooks).
practicalImplications: Became the universal standard for fine-tuning open-source LLMs (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen) on consumer GPUs (e.g. RTX 3090 / 4090).
Enabled ecosystem proliferation of modular adapters on HuggingFace Hub (PEFT library).

keyEquationsOrTheorems.label: LoRA Forward Transformation
keyEquationsOrTheorems.formulaOrDescription:
h = W_0 * x + (alpha / r) * B * A * x
(W_0: Frozen Base Weights, B: Matrix [d x r], A: Matrix [r x k], alpha: Scaling Constant)

keyEquationsOrTheorems.label: Adapter Weight Merge Condition
keyEquationsOrTheorems.formulaOrDescription:
W_deployed = W_0 + (alpha / r) * (B * A)
(Enables zero-latency direct inference deployment)

strengths: Zero inference latency penalty when merged into weights.
Drastic reduction in GPU memory and checkpoint storage.
Retains base model general knowledge while enabling domain specialization.
weaknesses: Cannot memorize vast amounts of net-new factual knowledge compared to full continuous pre-training.
potentialBiases: Evaluated primarily on English NLP task benchmarks.

title: Gravitational Microlensing
abstract: Gravitational microlensing is a unique planet-detection method that does not rely on detecting light from the host star or planet. Instead, planets are discovered when their gravitational field perturbs the light coming from a distant source. The mechanics of this method offer several advantages. It has the ability to detect wide-orbit planets of various masses around host stars of different types, at and beyond the system's snow line. Thus, microlensing complements the other detecting techniques that are more sensitive to close-orbit or high-mass planets. In this Chapter, we review the microlensing method and discuss how the physical properties, such as mass and distance, can be extracted from the microlensing light curve or from additional high-angular resolution observations. Microlensing is essential for the broader context of exoplanet demographics, as it can place constraints on planets, in wide orbits, beyond the {\it snow line}. Studying this parameter space can help us unravel the details of planet formation and how our own Solar System formed. Lastly, we provide an example of how to model a light curve and obtain accurate physical parameters for the host and planet.

Gravitational Microlensing

October 9, 2026
Abstract
Gravitational microlensing is a unique planet-detection method that does not rely on detecting
light from the host star or planet. Instead, planets are discovered when their gravitational field
perturbs the light coming from a distant source. The mechanics of this method offer several
advantages. It has the ability to detect wide-orbit planets of various masses around host stars
of different types, at and beyond the system’s snow line. Thus, microlensing complements the
other detecting techniques that are more sensitive to close-orbit or high-mass planets. In this
Chapter, we review the microlensing method and discuss how the physical properties, such as

sections.name: Introduction
sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Gravitational lensing is a phenomenon that occurs when light is deflected due to the gravitational field
of a massive body. Its origins stem from the theory of general relativity formulated by Albert Einstein
in the early twentieth century. However, the concept that gravity can bend light far precedes this,
with its roots tracing back to Sir Isaac Newton. In the early 1800s, the bending of light around the
Sun was calculated by Johann Georg von Soldner using Newtonian mechanics, but it was Einstein’s
theory of general relativity that provided a more complete description: that massive objects cause a
curvature in spacetime, and light follows this curvature.
Gravitational microlensing is a type of lensing where multiple images are created due to the de-
flection of light by gravity but have separations of less than a few milliarcseconds and are therefore
unresolved. The equations of microlensing by a foreground star aligning with a background star were
first published by Einstein in 1936 (Einstein, 1936). Additional published references to the phenomenon
of microlensing also exist (Chwolson, 1924; Eddington, 1920; Lodge, 1919). However, when Einstein
presented his derivations, he dismissed the practical significance of the microlensing effect, remarking
that “there is no great chance of observing this phenomenon” (Einstein, 1936).
Einstein’s pessimism, however, was based in truth: there is “no great chance” of observing a
gravitational microlensing event. The chance alignment between an observer, foreground star and
background star has a 10−6 probability of occurring when observing towards the Galactic Bulge (Alcock
et al., 2000), and can be even less for other lines of sight. This low probability partly contributed to
gravitational microlensing laying mostly dormant for decades (however, see Liebes 1964 and Refsdal
1964).
In 1986, however, a paper by Bohdan Paczy´nski resurrected the idea and the hunt for microlensing
events towards the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds and Galactic Bulge began in the early 1990s
(Alcock et al., 1993; Aubourg et al., 1993; Udalski et al., 1993). His idea was based on the new
developments being made in CCD detectors, which had larger field-of-views, enabling billions of stars
to be observed simultaneously every night. In 1991, Mao and Paczy´nski proposed that the microlensing
method could also be used to detect exoplanets. They predicted that 10% of the microlensing events
to-be observed could be binary-lens events, in which one of the lens components could be a planet
(Mao & Paczynski, 1991).
1

-- 1 of 50 --
The first microlensing surveys began in the early 1990’s with a primary goal of detecting dark
matter in our galaxy in the form of MAssive Compact Halo Objects (MACHOs). This gave birth to
the MACHO project (1992-1999,Alcock et al. 2000), along with the Exp´erience de Recherche d’Objects
Sombres (EROS, Aubourg et al., 1993) (1989-2003) and the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment
(OGLE, Udalski, 2003). All these collaborations detected microlensing events and placed constraints
on the number of Massive Compact Halo Objects in the Galaxy (see Alcock et al. 2000, Tisserand
et al. 2007 and Udalski et al. 1994).
In the early 2000s, the Microlensing Observations in Astrophysics (MOA, Sumi et al., 2013) col-
laboration joined forces with OGLE, searching for planetary systems. One of the earliest planetary
discoveries through microlensing was event OGLE-2003-BLG-235/MOA-2003-BLG-53 (Bond et al.,
2004), detected in July 2003 by OGLE’s 1.3m Warsaw telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in
Chile, and MOA’s 0.6 metre telescope at the Mt John observatory in New Zealand. In the mid-
2010s, a network of three wide-field telescopes distributed across the globe also joined the effort of
continuously monitoring the sky in search of microlensing events. The network, known as the Korea
Microlensing Telescope Network (KMTNet, Kim et al., 2016), has three 1.6 metre telescopes at the
Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), Chile; the South African Astronomical Observa-
tory (SAAO), South Africa; and at the Siding Spring Observatory (SSO) in Australia. In addition to
these surveys, the PRime-focus Infrared Microlensing Experiment (PRIME, Sumi et al., 2025) survey
began operations in 2023. Its 1.8m telescope at SAAO is the first dedicated wide-field near-infrared
microlensing survey telescope.
Continuously monitoring the Galactic Bulge, where stellar density is the highest, is crucial for
a microlensing event to be detected. However, the microlensing light curve also needs to be well-
sampled for useful information to be extracted. Once survey collaborations have detected an event,
the data is reduced in real time, and the event is alerted. This means that follow-up collaborations
can monitor these probable microlensing events. These teams include Probing Lensing Anomalies
NETwork (PLANET, Albrow et al., 1998), Robonet (Tsapras et al., 2009), Microlensing Network for
the Detection of Small Terrestrial Exoplanets (MiNDSTEp, Dominik et al., 2010), Microlensing Follow
Up Network (μFUN, Gould et al., 2010), and OMEGA (Bachelet et al., 2024).
In the following sections, we explain the microlensing method, with descriptions of a single lens and
binary lens system, in addition to how the physical parameters can be measured. We then discuss the
demographics of exoplanets discovered through microlensing, followed by an example of data analysis.
The different microlensing parameters that we discuss in this chapter can be found in Table 1.
2 Method Description
It is known that the gravitational field of an object can act similarly to an optical lens, magnifying
light from a background star. This phenomenon can produce multiple images for a single source, whose
number and characteristics depend on the configuration and properties of the lens system. Most mi-
crolensing events, however, do not produce resolvable images with current observational instruments.
Thus, the phenomenon is typically studied by analyzing the total magnification of these images by
monitoring the changes in brightness of the background star over time. Nevertheless, advanced interfer-
ometric observations, such as those performed with GRAVITY in 2019 (Dong et al., 2019), PIONIER in
2022 (Cassan et al., 2022), and GRAVITY in 2024 Wu et al. (2024) (the first resolution of microlensed
images of a binary-lens event), have succeeded in resolving microlensed images in exceptional cases.
In these observations, the main challenge lies not in angular resolution, but rather in the brightness of
the target and the availability of suitable nearby fringe-tracker stars.
Unlike other lensing effects, such as strong lensing, where the resulting images can persist for years,
planetary microlensing events typically last only a few weeks. Due to the relative motion of stars in
our Galaxy, different combinations of source stars and lens systems can become aligned over time,
enabling the observation of many different microlensing events. Observing regions with high stellar
density, such as the Galactic Bulge, significantly increases the likelihood of detecting such events and
is therefore preferred for microlensing-dedicated surveys.
For didactic purposes, this section organizes the description of the physics behind microlensing
according to the number of objects in the lens system. Table 1 presents the main parameters used in

2.1 Single Lens Event
As usual, the simplest scenario is that in which the lens system is composed of one object, as shown
in Figure 1. In the microlensing community, the lens is often denoted by L and the source by S, a
convention we follow throughout this Chapter. Accordingly, the distance from the observer to the lens
is denoted DL, and the distance from the observer to the source is DS. In the case of one object acting
as a lens, two images are created, denoted I+ and I−. When the source star and the lens object of
a microlensing event are infinitesimal points, this event is commonly called a point-source point-lens
(PSPL) event. A PSPL is a type of single-lens single-source (1L1S) event.
Modelling a microlensing event essentially involves determining the set of parameters that best
reproduce the observed magnification. Therefore, in this subsection, we walk through how we derive
the magnification (see Figure 2) of a PSPL event, considering the lensing geometry shown in Figure 1.

The magnification function is used to model the observed flux during a microlensing event. The
total flux for an instrument with a passband i at any given time t is expressed as:
Fi(t) = A · fs,i + fb,i (15)
where A is the derived magnification (equation 13) of the event at any given time and for any given set

its excess flux, accounting for blended light. The latter represents fluxes from other unrelated nearby
stars or objects along the line of sight of the observer to the microlensing system and is constant as it
is not affected by the lensing event.
Since microlensing is a highly sensitive effect, it is often necessary to consider that the source star
is not a point source, which is referred to in microlensing as a finite source. This type of 1L1S event
is named a finite-source point-lens (FSPL) event. The microlensing effect causes the images of the
source to appear more or less distorted depending on how close the source approaches the lens from the
observer’s viewpoint. This effect is illustrated in Figure 3, where the contour of the source is mapped
and its image is calculated in the lens plane. See Section 2.4.1 for more details.
Exoplanet detection has traditionally focused on bound planets, which for microlensing detection
involves a multi-lens system. Even so, the Paczy´nski curve remains very relevant, as many planetary
microlensing events are initially identified using PSPL or single-lens search techniques before being
further modelled as multi-lens systems. Moreover, single-lens models are particularly valuable for
detecting free-floating planets (FFPs) (Sumi et al., 2023) as well as neutron stars and stellar-mass
black holes (Lam et al., 2022). It is also worth noting that a wide-orbit planet could orbit far enough
from its host star to appear as an FFP. See Section 3 for more information on exoplanet demographics
with microlensing.

2.2 Binary Lens Event
During a microlensing event, multiple objects can collectively act as a lens. Common lensing systems
include combinations such as two stars, a star and a planet, a star with two planets, two stars with
a planet, star and Brown dwarf, or Brown dwarf binaries - all of which can magnify the light from a
background star. Among these, a binary lens system composed of a star and a planet is, nowadays,
the most frequently observed type for exoplanet detection in microlensing studies. An event involving
two lenses and one source is referred to as a binary-lens single-source (2L1S) event, while an event
with two lenses and two sources is referred to as a binary-lens binary-source (2L2S) event.
According to the International Astronomical Union, any object that orbits stars, brown dwarfs,
or stellar remnants and has a mass ratio of q < 2/(25 + √621) ≈ 0.04 qualifies as an exoplanet
(Des Etangs & Lissauer, 2022). Therefore, a binary lens event where the mass ratio q is significantly
small is usually considered a planetary microlensing event, which is of primary interest to the exoplanet
research community. Importantly, microlensing naturally provides a direct measurement of the lens
mass ratio q, and the recent adoption of a mass-ratio-based definition of planets further emphasizes
the physical significance of this parameter in planet formation scenarios. This reflects a significant
conceptual shift, as the mass ratio itself is used to identify the planetary nature of the secondary
body in the lens system, whereas converting mass ratios into absolute masses was previously thought
necessary to determine the nature of the secondary lens.

Currently, there is no analytical solution for the magnification resulting from a binary lens system.
However, the lens equation can be solved numerically. The conjugate of Equation 17 can be rearranged
and z substituted back into the same equation, allowing the binary lens equation to be rewritten as a
fifth-order complex polynomial in z (Witt, 1990; Witt & Mao, 1995). The five polynomial coefficients,
detailed in Witt & Mao (1995), enable the numerical determination of five roots. Note that these
solutions do not always correspond to physical images of the source (Rhie, 1997; Witt, 1990; Witt &
Mao, 1995). In particular, sources located outside a caustic loop produce three images, whereas sources
inside the caustic loop produce five images (Rhie, 1997; Witt, 1990). To determine whether a root
of the fifth-order polynomial corresponds to a physical image, the solution must be checked against
the original lens equation. This is because the polynomial equation is implied by the lens equation,
but is not equivalent to it, as the equivalence is lost during the mathematical derivation (Rhie, 1997;
Schneider & Weiss, 1986; Witt, 1990).
As in the case with single lenses, the magnification of the background star is calculated by A = 1
detJ .
The set of source positions where detJ = 0 defines what is known as caustic curves (Gaudi, 2012).
Note that in the point-source approximation, the magnification formally diverges when the source
lies exactly on a caustic. However, real stars have a finite angular size, so different regions of the
stellar disc experience different magnifications when the source is crossing or approaching a caustic.
The observed magnification, therefore, corresponds to the surface-brightness-weighted average over the
source profile, which smooths the formal divergence predicted by the point-source approximation and

For a binary lens system, caustic curves are of critical importance because they mark the boundaries
within the source plane where multiple images (three or five) are created. The caustic curves in a
binary lens system are defined by this new set of parameters: the mass ratio q, which represents the
ratio between the secondary lens and the primary lens, and the projected separation s between the two
lenses, which is normalized by the Einstein radius θE. We usually define three caustic topologies: close,
intermediate/resonant, and wide, which are defined by the shape of the curves themselves. As shown
in Figure 4, the close topology is composed of a central four-cusped caustic along with two planetary
three-cusped caustics. The resonant topology consists of a single central six-cusped caustic. The wide
topology includes a central four-cusped caustic and a planetary four-cusped caustic. Figure 4(b) shows
how the caustic topology varies as a function of the projected lens separation s and mass ratio q. The
topology transition limits are given in Dominik (1999), where sw is the wide–resonant separation limit

While the caustic topology is determined by s and q, modelling the event also requires describing
the trajectory of the source relative to the lens system. A third parameter is introduced: the angle α,
which measures the angle between the relative motion of the source and the line connecting the two
masses of the binary lens system, typically measured counter-clockwise. For planetary microlensing
events, the primary lens is typically the host star, while the secondary lens is the planet. As mentioned
previously, finite-source effects play an important role in binary-lensing models and must therefore be
included. These effects can be explicitly included as the normalized size of the source ρ∗, or implicitly
through the parameter t∗, which represents the time required for the source radius to cross the Einstein
radius of the lens. This relationship is given by t∗ = ρ∗ · tE.

2.3 Triple Lens Event
As previously mentioned, multiple objects can collectively act as a lens during a microlensing event.
We have already discussed the binary lens case, where either a stellar binary or a star + planet act as
the lens. Now we will discuss the more complicated case of a triple lens event, in this case, a triple-lens
single-source (3L1S). This can involve one planet orbiting two stars, two planets orbiting one star, or
even a planet and an exomoon orbiting a star.

masses M1 and M2. The total deflection of light must then include the contribution from this additional

peaks and troughs.
Triple lens events still represent a relatively small fraction of detected microlensing events, and
modelling techniques for these more complex systems remain computationally challenging and are
still under active development. Nevertheless, detections of these systems are increasing (Danˇek &

2.4 Characterising Lens System Parameters
One distinguishing factor of microlensing compared to other exoplanet detection techniques is that
host or lens stars are not observed directly. Additionally, these stars are often faint, or their light
is blended with other stars, especially when observing towards the Galactic bulge, one of the most
densely populated regions in our galaxy. This means that routine observables from the microlensing
event do not directly yield physical properties, such as mass and distance, of the planetary system
beyond the planet/star mass ratio q, and projected separation s. This lack of information hinders our
ability to make statistical comparisons between the frequency of planets found in microlensing surveys
and those detected by other planet search methods. Overcoming this limitation has been a major

Several second-order effects can be present and measured on a microlensing light curve that deviates

observers. When either of these assumptions fail, it is generally termed microlens parallax (πE) and it
is a two-dimensional vector with north and east components (πE,N , πE,E ).
This can manifest in three ways: orbital parallax occurs when the timescale of a microlensing event
lasts a significant fraction of a year (> 80 days). Coupled with the acceleration of the Earth, this can

the Einstein ring due to their different perspectives (Gould et al., 2009). These different perspectives
will cause changes in the observed magnifications. This effect is exacerbated for sources that are close
to a caustic and are therefore highly magnified (Holz & Wald, 1996).

tion of the Einstein ring radius projected in the observer plane. This can happen when a microlensing
event is simultaneously observed from Earth and a satellite in a solar orbit (Udalski et al., 2015). The
two observers will see significant differences in magnification (Gould, 1994a).

2.4.2 High-Angular Resolution Follow-up Observations
Obtaining the physical properties of the lens system from second-order effects on the light curve can
sometimes prove to be tricky, since they are often prone to degeneracies. Furthermore, to obtain
robust measurements of the lens properties, one would need at least two mass-distance relations.
high-angular resolution follow-up observations allow us to directly observe the lens star - which is
not possible during the microlensing event when the source, lens and observer are aligned. These
observations are typically taken with large ground-based telescopes with adaptive optics capabilities
(such as Keck I and II, Wizinowich et al. 2000, or Subaru, Luo et al. 2010, on Mauna Kea, Hawai’i),
or with space-based telescopes such as the Hubble Space Telescope (Hubble, Zimmerman, 2010) or the
James Webb Space Telescope (Webb, Gardner et al., 2006). These powerful telescopes can resolve or
partially resolve the source and lens, enabling us to directly measure the lens flux and relative proper
motion (magnitude and direction) to the source.
Lens Flux: High resolution follow-up observations are typically taken in the near-infrared bands,
such as J (λcentral = 1.25μm), K (λcentral = 1.65μm), and H (λcentral = 2.2μm) from ground-based
telescopes. These passbands suffer less extinction compared to optical wavelengths as they can more
effectively penetrate the interstellar dust between us and the Galactic centre. A measured magnitude
of the lens star can yield the following mass-distance relation:
KL = 10 + 5log10(DL/1kpc) + MK(ML) + AK,L, (29)
where MK(ML) is a mass-luminosity relation in the K passband (but can be substituted for any
passband), and AK,L is the dust extinction in the foreground of the lens star. Empirical mass-luminosity
relations for a main sequence star are appropriate in the majority of cases. Examples of empirical
mass-luminosity relations are from Henry & McCarthy (1993) (ML ≥ 0.66 M⊙), Delfosse et al. (2000)
(0.54 M⊙ ≥ ML ≥ 0.12 M⊙) and Henry et al. (1999) (0.10 M⊙ ≥ ML ≥ 0.07 M⊙). However, for
host stars ∼ 1M⊙ whose luminosity may change substantially over the age of the Galaxy, isochrones
are likely to be more accurate (e.g. Girardi et al., 2002). Measurements of the lens flux in multiple
passbands can give independent mass and distance estimates.
Relative Proper Motion: When the peak of the microlensing event has passed, the source and lens
are no longer aligned. Depending on their relative proper motion (how many arcseconds per year they
move apart relative to each other), follow-up observations can be taken ∼3-10 years after the peak of the
event to resolve or partially resolve the lens. This can also happen in reverse if high-resolution images
of the lens and source were taken before the microlensing event took place. In high-resolution imaging,
therefore, the relative proper motion can be calculated by measuring the source-lens separation as

3 Demographics of the Detected Planets
Thousands of planets have been discovered to date using all the different detection techniques, and
tens of thousands more are expected to be discovered as space-based technology improves. Only a
couple hundred of these planets, however, have been discovered by gravitational microlensing since it
relies on the chance alignment between the source, lens, and observer. Another limitation is that of
the detected planetary systems, obtaining precise and reliable measurements of mass and distance can
be challenging, as outlined in Section 2.4. A major reason for this is that the detection does not rely
on the host or companion’s light, and although this poses some challenges, it also comes with several
advantages.
Microlensing observations provide important tests of planet formation models because they are
sensitive to planets in wide orbits across a broad range of masses. For example, Suzuki et al. (2018)
found substantially more intermediate-mass giant planets than predicted by standard core accretion
models, suggesting that current theories of planet formation may be incomplete.
Each exoplanet detection method has its strengths, with microlensing uniquely suited to detecting
low-mass planets in wide orbits around a diverse range of host stars. Additionally, it is currently the
only method capable of probing planetary populations far beyond the solar neighbourhood toward
the Galactic centre. In the following subsections, we outline the regions of parameter space to which
microlensing is sensitive.
3.1 Wide Orbit ‘Cold’ Planets
The probability of detecting a planet with microlensing is maximised when the planet projected separa-
tion from its host star is approximately equal to the Einstein radius of the lensing system, rE = DLθE.
This is the radius of the Einstein ring image, which is seen when the lens and source are in perfect
alignment and where lensing effects are the strongest. When a planet is near the Einstein radius, its
gravitational influence will call a deviation, or planetary anomaly, on the light curve. The Einstein
radius for typical microlensing events will correspond to a physical distance of 1-5 AU for solar mass
lenses towards the Galactic centre. Planets with a projected separation equal to these distances are
more likely to be detected, as the sensitivity peaks at the Einstein radius of the host star (Bennett &
Rhie, 1996; Gould & Loeb, 1992; Mao & Paczynski, 1991). Planets with smaller orbital separations lie
well within the Einstein radius, and therefore their lensing signal is weaker or often indistinguishable
from the host star’s lensing effect. Therefore, these planets are harder to detect with gravitational
microlensing. Planets that lie beyond the Einstein radius (so even greater separation from the host
star) can be detected, although the probability decreases the further away the planet gets.
For many planetary systems, this Einstein radius distance (1-5 AU) is expected to coincide with the
region beyond the protoplanetary disk (Gould & Loeb, 1992). This is where temperatures are below
the ideal temperature of water in its liquid form, therefore earning its name as the snow line. Planets
at or beyond the snow line are typically referred to as ‘cold’ planets. In the right panel of Figure 13 we
see that many planets found with microlensing are estimated to be orbiting beyond their system’s snow

3.2 Free Floating Planets
Free-floating (or ‘rogue’) planets are objects that do not orbit any star, and these elusive objects can
be detected with gravitational microlensing (Stefano & Scalzo, 1999). Rogue planets have two possible
ways of forming. They could either form in isolation, where they would assemble through a similar
process to star formation (Whitworth & Stamatellos, 2006), or they could form around a star, initially
bound, and only later escape its host’s gravitational field (Sumi et al., 2011; Veras & Raymond, 2012).
Planets can be ejected from their hosts gravitational field in a number of ways. This can be the result
of chaotic processes during planet formation (e.g. Rasio & Ford, 1996), stellar flybys (e.g. Malmberg
et al., 2011), or when the host enters its post main sequence stage (e.g. Adams & Bloch, 2013).
The survey collaborations MOA, OGLE and KMTNet have a sufficiently high enough cadence to
detect isolated microlensing events, in addition to planetary events. Microlensing events with short
time scales (∼1 day long) were identified and studied, with the results indicating that there could be
a substantial population of Jupiter-mass rogue planets, with an abundance of ∼2 rogue Jupiter-mass
planets per star in the Galaxy. These short time scale events can be found in Sumi et al. (2011), with
the search being expanded in Sumi et al. (2023) with MOA-II survey data collected between 2006
and 2014. They found six short-duration microlensing events likely to be caused by rogue planets.
Koshimoto et al. (2023) using the same data also discovered low-mass rogue planet candidates. They
analysed thousands of single lens microlensing event candidates, singling out thirteen very short-
duration events which could be caused by low-mass rogue planets. Since these short duration events
caused by low-mass objects are very difficult to detect, their results suggested that there may actually
be a very large population of low-mass rogue planets in our galaxy.

3.3 Low-Mass Planets
When a background source’s light is magnified by a planetary lens system, the magnitude of the
perturbation on the light curve due to the planet does not depend on the planet’s mass. Instead, it
depends on how close the source’s light passes the planetary caustics. If the source passes very close
or crosses the planetary caustics, it can cause a very large perturbation. As the mass of the planet
decreases, planetary deviations also become rarer and briefer, but the magnitude of the perturbation
can still be large for the background source. Therefore, microlensing can be sensitive to low-mass
planets (Bennett & Rhie, 1996).
Although the full picture of low-mass planet demographics is yet to be seen, a number of studies
have been conducted in the last decade, probing the detection efficiency and mass function of planets
identified through microlensing. A study by Cassan et al. (2012) found that planets with lower masses,
particularly in the super-Earth to sub-Neptune range (5-15 M⊕), were relatively common at wider
orbits (1-10 AU). Furthermore, they estimated that planets are, in general, abundant in our Galaxy,
with at least one planet per star.

Another prominent study in microlensing is by Suzuki et al. (2016). They studied the planet-host
mass-ratio for a number of microlensing events, finding that the mass-ratio function breaks and peaks
at q ∼ 10−4 for planets in wide orbits. This implies that cold Neptune mass planets are the most
frequently detected by microlensing, which contradicts the prediction made by Laughlin et al. (2004)
of a sub-Saturn desert for wide-orbit planets. However, further investigation with more precise and
independent measurements of both planet and host star masses (rather than just the mass-ratio) is
essential for a clearer understanding.
Low-mass planets, down to Earth or even Mars still remain hard to detect with ground-based
microlensing. This is because ground-based observations have a limited resolution, making short or
faint deviations in the light curve difficult to capture. The upcoming Roman mission is expected
to uncover a substantial population of terrestrial-mass planets through its space-based microlensing
survey.
3.4 Host Star demographics
Due to gravitational lensing’s unique nature, microlensing can detect planets orbiting a variety of host
stars, or host objects, from brown dwarfs to black holes.
This is a consequence of the technique not relying on the light emitted by the lensing object.
Microlensing relies only on the gravitational field of the lens, not its luminosity. This means that even
very faint or non-luminous objects, such as brown dwarfs, white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes,
can act as lenses (e.g. Lam et al., 2022; Sahu et al., 2022) and potentially host a planet. Blackman
et al. (2021) report the possible discovery of the first wide-orbit planet around a white dwarf, providing
evidence that planets in such systems can survive both the giant and asymptotic giant phases of their
host star’s evolution. Such detection proved that microlensing is a method that can also detect older
planetary systems that have evolved off the main sequence. Low-mass stars are far more numerous in
our Galaxy than high-mass stars, which is why microlensing surveys have detected large numbers of
them, making microlensing an ideal method for their discovery. Moreover, the Einstein crossing time
scales with the square root of the lens mass, tE ∝ √M , so events caused by low-mass stars have shorter
durations. Surveys such as OGLE, MOA, KMTNet, and the forthcoming Roman Space Telescope are
designed with sufficiently high cadences to remain sensitive to these short-timescale events.
One characteristic that needs to be explored further is the occurrence rate of planets that orbit
beyond the snow line as a function of host star mass. For example, at these wider orbits, are more
massive stars more likely to host more massive planets? Studies with Kepler data, for planets in short
orbits, have indicated there is a significant difference in planet occurrence for M dwarfs compared to
solar type stars with spectral types F, G, and K (Mulders et al., 2015). However, a different trend is
expected for planets beyond their host star’s snow line. Laughlin et al. (2004) suggests that massive
planets, such as gas giants, will form more easily around more massive stars. Moreover, they suggest
that the protoplanetary disks of smaller stars, such as M-dwarfs, will dissipate their Hydrogen and
Helium before they can be accreted onto protoplanets to form gas giants. However, microlensing has
detected several systems with gas giants orbiting M dwarfs (e.g. Bennett et al., 2020; Bennett et al.,
2024; Dong et al., 2009; Poleski et al., 2014; Tsapras et al., 2014), indicating that the formation of gas
giants around M dwarfs could be more plausible than previously predicted.
Most of the planets detected so far have been at distances < 1 kpc from Earth. Microlensing is
currently the only technique that can detect planetary systems towards the Galactic centre. This gives
us the opportunity to study lenses in both the disk and Galactic bulge, which can be seen in Figure
15. A study by Koshimoto et al. (2021b) using microlensing data to investigate the distribution of
exoplanets at varying distances to the Galactic centre found that there is no significant dependence of
planet occurrence on the Galactocentric distance. This implies that cold planets—those most readily
detectable via microlensing—are fairly uniformly distributed across the Galaxy, including within the
Galactic bulge. Therefore, planet formation processes might be similarly effective across different
galactic environments, from the dense stellar populations of the bulge to the sparser outer regions of
the disk.
Due to the limitations that microlensing faces, it is difficult to determine the stellar ages, surface
temperatures, and spectral types of the host stars. Follow-up observations of the host star could
address this once the source and lens are resolved. Observations would also have to be taken in
multiple band-widths in both the near-infrared and visible, so that accurate colour information can be

3.5 Circumbinary Systems
A system that involves a planet orbiting a pair of stars in close orbit is called a circumbinary system.
Although microlensing is sensitive to such systems, the detection of them can be challenging due to the
complex nature of their light curves, and the precise alignment that needs to occur. The first confirmed
circumbinary system detected via microlensing is OGLE-2007-BLG-349 (Bennett et al., 2016), which
consists of a 80 M⊕ planet orbiting a pair of M-dwarfs. More recently, Han et al. (2020) analysed
OGLE-2018-BLG-1700, finding that the system consists of a planet that belongs to a stellar binary
system. The system’s triple lens nature (two host stars and a planet) was identified from the complex
anomaly pattern of the light curve (see Figure 16).
Modelling such systems requires the use of triple-lens modelling (Rhie, 1997), described in Section
2.3. The light curve models of triple-lens systems appear more complex, as all objects in the lensing
system perturb the light from the background source. In Figures 16 and 17 we show examples of the
complex nature of triple-lens light curves.
The discovery of these types of systems has large implications for understanding planet formation.
3.6 Multi-planet Systems
Although rare, microlensing has also detected systems with multiple planets (i.e. multiple planets
orbiting one star). It is rare to detect these systems with microlensing because all planets in the
system would need to significantly perturb the light curve, and the chance alignment required to
detect a single planet is already small. Nevertheless, such detections are possible if the planets are
within the lensing zone and affect the magnification pattern of the light curve (Griest & Safizadeh,
1998).
The first published multi-planet event in microlensing is OGLE-2006-BLG-109, which has a Jupiter
and Saturn mass planet orbiting a 0.5 M⊙ star (Bennett et al., 2010; Gaudi et al., 2008). Modelling
these multi-planet events requires triple lens modelling, similar to what is used in circumbinary systems.
However, instead of one planet orbiting two host stars, we have two planets orbiting one host star (see
Section 2.3). Triple lens events are often signified by complex light curves that have many features
(spikes and troughs) exhibited.

with microlensing.
4 Example of Data Analysis
When talking about gravitational microlensing data analysis, we can summarize it in three main
procedures: (1) identifying potential events through variations in stellar brightness; (2) modelling the
event’s light curve to extract details about the lens; and (3) measuring the lens’ mass through follow-up
or precursor observations. The third step is optional and only required when finite source effects are
not enough to yield accurate estimates of the physical parameters by themselves. In this section, we
provide a summary of these processes.

These three main procedures are typically performed in a particular order (see Figure 18). First,
you must identify the event using data from the various microlensing surveys. The event selection
process is described in more detail in the following subsection. Subsequently, the light curve modelling
can ensue. In this step, you can determine whether the event is a single-lens or binary-lens, and find
the model parameters. The physical parameters can be determined if there are significant higher order
effects on the light curve, or estimated using Galactic models with priors. Alternatively, after waiting
several years for the source and lens to no longer be aligned, the lens can be imaged directly high
angular resolution telescopes. This can also be achieved prior to the microlensing event itself. For
example, a Galactic field may be imaged with a high angular resolution telescope in anticipation of
ongoing or future microlensing surveys in that region. Once a microlensing event is identified, these
high-resolution precursor observations can be used to directly detect the lens star before it becomes
closely aligned with the source.
Direct measurements of the lens flux, and relative proper motion to the source, can be used as
constraints in the light curve model. Remodelling the light curve, with these constraints can help
reveal if the light curve is the best fit model, break degeneracies in the light curve model (if they
exist), and get more accurate model parameters (like, tE or q, for example).
In the following sections, we present data analysis examples for microlensing. We present the light
curve modelling of event MOA-2020-BLG-135, and the physical parameters which were determined
using the light curve model parameters and a Galactic model with priors (Ishitani Silva et al., 2022).
Furthermore, we describe the process of analysing Keck high resolution data, using MOA-2013-BLG-
220 (Vandorou et al., 2020), as an example.
4.1 Event Selection
Gravitational microlensing events are quite rare. Therefore, to detect a microlensing exoplanet, mil-
lions of stars in regions of high stellar density must be monitored simultaneously and continuously
over extended periods at a high cadence. Thanks to MOA, OGLE, KMTNet, and now PRIME, hun-
dreds of microlensing event candidates and dozens of new microlensing exoplanets are identified each
year. Given the large number of stars observed, a selection method is needed to identify potential mi-
crolensing occurrences. Although different collaborations may use slightly varied approaches, the most
common method involves detecting events with magnification and then fitting a PSPL microlensing
model to verify the likelihood that the light curve contains a microlensing event. From there, further

In the case of the MOA collaboration, the detection process begins by identifying significant bright-
ness amplifications in stars, which may indicate the gravitational lensing of a background object. Since
the Galactic bulge is highly crowded, MOA uses real-time difference imaging analysis, where a high-
quality reference image is subtracted from subsequent observations to isolate only variable flux (Bond
et al., 2001). This technique allows small brightness variations to be detected even when individual
stars are not fully resolved. It scans for positive or negative point spread function (PSF) profiles,
depending on brightness changes, and retains objects with a signal-to-noise ratio greater than five.
This step filters out cosmic rays and other artificial effects. Cosmic rays do not exhibit PSF shapes
and do not recur as consecutive events. Next, light curves are built and checked within a window to
confirm a steady baseline flux. Events that display a consistent brightening pattern across at least
three consecutive measurements are retained, eliminating other non-microlensing variations. This is
necessary to ensure that selected light curves show clear and steady brightening events. Then, a PSPL
model is fitted to the candidates to verify that each event’s behavior is consistent with that of a real
microlensing event. The PSPL fitting is necessary to eliminate events that can resemble microlensing,
such as moving objects, cataclysmic variables, and supernovae. When fitting a PSPL, such events
usually produce a high χ2 and / or unphysical values of parameters (Sumi et al., 2011, 2013). It is
possible that with additional data points or further analysis, the alerted transient candidates may be
identified as non-microlensing.
Collaborations like MOA, OGLE, and KMTNet alert to possible microlensing events on their
websites. MOA alerts are available at: https://moaprime.massey.ac.nz/moaarchive; while the OGLE
warning system is accessible at: https://ogle.astrouw.edu.pl/ogle4/ews/ews.html; and KMTNet light
curves are available at: https://kmtnet.kasi.re.kr/ ulens/. These websites provide quick access to
light curves with initial PSPL fits and results. Table 3 provides a list of main telescopes used by the
gravitational microlensing community.
Due to the large number of light curves to analyze, the quick PSPL fit serves as a preliminary
step before performing a more detailed binary or triple lens analysis. With the help of the PSPL fit,
microlensing experts often identify interesting light curves with potential planetary signatures, either
by visual inspection or through computational tools, such as the publicly available RTModel (Bozza,
2024a). Binary or triple lens models are then applied to these selected candidates. See Section 4.2 for
more modelling information.
Over the years, alternative approaches have been developed to select interesting microlensing, many
of them implementing machine learning techniques (Chu et al., 2019; Gezer et al., 2022; Godines et al.,
2019; Ishitani Silva, 2023; Mr´oz, 2020; Wyrzykowski et al., 2016). Nevertheless, PSPL fitting remains

4.2 Light Curve Modelling
The goal of light curve modelling is to determine the physical parameters that best explain the observed
data. There are many open-source tools available for light curve modelling; see Table 4 for a list.
In scientific modelling, it is easy to overcomplicate the model by adding unnecessary parameters.
To avoid this, we always begin with the simplest model, which in the case of microlensing, is a single
source and a single lens. From there, we gradually add complexity, introducing additional objects such
as another lens or a secondary source.
To illustrate the modelling process, we use the example of MOA-2020-BLG-135Lb, a planetary
event whose discovery and modelling analysis were reported in Ishitani Silva et al. (2022). The paper
is open access, and the data used for the analysis are also available within the paper, along with a
link in the first figure of the paper. For this published event, the modelling was performed using
the eesunhong software (Bennett & Rhie, 1996), and the outputs were analyzed with the MOAna
software (Ranc, 2020). Although eesunhong is now publicly available on GitHub (https://github.
com/golmschenk/eesunhong), its documentation is still a work in progress and may be more suitable
for experienced microlensing researchers. As an alternative, we have prepared a publicly available
package that combines RTModel (Bozza, 2024a) for identifying initial conditions and pyLIMA (Bachelet
et al., 2017) for the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis. This package, designed for easier
use by newcomers, can be found at https://github.com/stelais/mb20135. For other open-source
tools, please also refer to Table 4.
For microlensing exoplanets, the event name can provide significant information. The event was
named to indicate that it was first discovered by the MOA collaboration using data from the MOA tele-
scope, a purpose-built 1.8 metre wide-field telescope located at Mount John Observatory, New Zealand.
Its first alert was issued in July 2020. Located at Galactic coordinates (l, b) = (0.15598◦, −1.95678◦),
the event was observed as the telescope pointed toward the Galactic bulge (BLG). This was the
135th alert issued by the collaboration in that year. Since microlensing events involve at least two
objects, the lens and the source, it is important to specify which one is or contains the planet. In this
case, the lens system is denoted by L, and the planet, as a secondary lens, is indicated by an addi-
tional b. Thus, the microlensing event is named MOA-2020-BLG-135, and the exoplanet discovered is
MOA-2020-BLG-135Lb.
The observed data are shown in Figure 19. In addition to the MOA-Red filter, which corresponds
to a customized wide bandwidth from 600 nm to 900 nm, the event was also observed in the visual
band using the MOA-V filter. Furthermore, the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) on Mauna
Kea, Hawaii, observed the event in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey i-band filter. It is noteworthy
that the light curve closely resembles a single-lens model with an additional bump in the interval
HJD′ = [9040.7, 9041.5]1, making the event likely to trigger alert systems that rely on single-lens

4.2.1 Single Lens, Single Source
A PSPL fitting is a type of 1L1S model defined by three primary parameters: the Einstein crossing
time, tE, the time of minimum separation, t0, and the minimum angular separation, u0. Although
collaborations provide preliminary PSPL models, it is important to start by rerunning them, to ensure
that all potential local minima are found.
The most common approach to fitting the observed light curve is to perform a grid search over
the parameters tE, t0, and u0 to identify the optimal model parameters. Because PSPL models are
computationally fast and have relatively few parameters, grid search remains a practical and effective
method to optimize this model. For events similar to MOA-2020-BLG-135, PSPL fitting results offer
great initial conditions for more complex models, such as binary lens or binary source fittings.
Due to the finite size of the source and the limb-darkening effect, an additional parameter, the
normalized angular radius ρ∗ (alternatively t∗, as t∗ = ρ∗tE) — can be introduced. This model is
referred to as a FSPL model. Both eesunhong, the code used in the published analysis, and RTModel,

4.2.2 Binary Lens, Single Source
A binary-lens single-source model, also referred to as 2L1S, represents a lens system composed of two
masses. The simplest form of the 2L1S model introduces three additional parameters: the ratio of the
secondary lens mass to the primary lens mass, q (or alternatively, the mass fraction ϵ), the separation
between the two lens components, s, and the counter-clockwise angle between the lens-source relative
motion and the binary lens axis, α.
When fitting a 2L1S model to the observed light curve, different researchers use varying approaches
as the first step. A common first step is to perform a grid search again, but now with tE, t0, u0, and ρ∗
(or t∗) fixed based on the 1L1S best-fit model, while scanning over s, α, and q. This process helps to
find initial conditions for the local minima. To ensure that no optimal model is overlooked, different
strategies are employed. For instance, Ishitani Silva et al. (2022) ensures that the mass ratios within
the range q ∈ [10−5, 10−1] are included in the set of initial conditions. In contrast, software such as
RTModel (Bozza, 2024a) takes a different approach to the grid search for this step. Instead, first, it

initial values for the separation s and mass ratio q based on the angular distance of the anomaly from
the primary lens. If the anomaly is large, it likely indicates a binary star lens system, where the mass
ratio q is large. In such cases, RTModel matches pre-defined templates with the characteristic double-
peaked structure. Once an initial guess is selected, RTModel performs a downhill minimization using
the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm (Marquardt, 1963) to locate a local minimum of the χ2 function
(Bozza, 2024a).
Once the initial conditions are identified, a MCMC algorithm is used to explore the full parameter
space and perform a complete fit, with all parameters allowed to vary freely. Both eesunhong, which
was used for the published event analysis, and pyLIMA, available in the online material, implement
MCMC methods with a variety of samplers. Then, the best-fit model is selected by looking for the
lowest χ2, which in that case indicated a model with q ∼ 10−4. Figure 20 shows the full parameter

4.2.3 Binary Source Possibility
The possibility of a binary source is also commonly explored, as it can produce features resembling
planetary signals. This scenario can be investigated using different lens systems, such as a single lens
and binary lens referred to as single-lens binary-source (1L2S) and 2L2S, respectively.
Because there are now two sources, we must take into consideration the impact parameter of the
primary source u01 and the impact parameter of the secondary source u02, as well as the time of the
minimum separation for the primary source t01 and for the secondary source t02. The new model still
includes tE and now adds the flux ratio FR of the secondary source to the primary source for each of
the observed passbands. The fitting procedure is similar to the other models, usually starting with a
grid search and followed by an MCMC.
It is important to note that adding more parameters to a model can often reduce the χ2 value
simply due to increased model flexibility. As a result, a lower χ2 does not necessarily indicate a
better or more appropriate model when comparing models with different numbers of parameters. To
properly evaluate model quality, additional model selection criteria are necessary. In addition to the χ2
comparison, (Ishitani Silva et al., 2022) used the Bayesian Information Criterion (Schwarz, 1978), which
penalizes models with more parameters. Alternatively, the software RTModel applies Wilks’ theorem
(Wilks, 1938) to evaluate the statistical significance of the χ2 improvement, and then determine the
minimum threshold differences for model selection.

4.2.4 Lens System Parameters Post-light Curve modelling
Light curve models of planetary events provide the mass ratio q, but they do not directly provide
the planet’s mass or its distance from Earth. To solve that, one approach is to determine the host
star’s mass by observing the system when the separation between the source and lens is large enough
to make such observations possible. This method is discussed in Section 4.3. However, during the
detection of the event, the lens and source are too close to allow for such measurements. Consequently,
alternative methods must be employed to estimate the properties of the lens system. Galactic models,
such as those presented by Bennett et al. (2014) and Koshimoto et al. (2021a), offer a valuable tool
for estimating key lens system parameters, including its distance and mass.
The work for the presented example reported the results using Bennett et al. (2014)’s Galactic
model with two different priors. Assuming that all stars have equal probability of hosting a planet,

It’s worth noting that in most microlensing studies, the Galactic prior is applied after the light
curve modelling stage rather than incorporated directly into the parameter-space exploration. While
including the Galactic model self-consistently during the fit would be more rigorous mathematically,
this is computationally challenging because the prior depends on parameters such as tE, which vary
throughout the exploration of parameter space. As a result, Galactic Bayesian analyses are typically
performed as a post-processing step following the determination of the best-fit microlensing model.
More sophisticated analyses incorporating additional constraints, such as high-resolution imaging, can
instead perform a more self-consistent joint modelling of the light curve and lens properties.
4.3 Lens System Mass Measurement
Once a microlensing event has been modelled, the next step is to try and determine the lens system’s
physical parameters. These include host star mass, distance, planet mass, and projected separation.
In Section 2.4 we go over all the possible ways in which a mass-distance relation can be obtained.
Many of these include the presence of higher order effects on the light curve - such as, parallax, orbital
motion, xallarap or binary source effects. Additionally, one can obtain mass-distance relations from
directly observing the lens flux and measuring its relative proper motion to the source, once they are
no longer aligned. In this section, we outline the steps required to make direct lens flux and relative
proper motion measurements with high-angular resolution data.
We take the example of MOA-2013-BLG-220, a planetary event initially modelled and published
in Yee et al. (2014). High-angular resolution observations were taken with Keck 6 years after the
peak of the microlensing event, resolving the source and lens. The data and analysis are presented in
Vandorou et al. (2020). The following example uses publicly available Keck data from KOA - the Keck
Observatory Archive. Example python notebooks using the MOA-2013-BLG-220 data can be found
at https://github.com/KatieVandorou/MB13220-Example-Analysis.
4.3.1 Keck Data
Follow-up observations for microlensing events are typically taken with Keck I’s OH-Suppressing In-
frared Imaging Spectrograph (OSIRIS) instrument, or with Keck II’s Near Infrared Camera Second
Generation (NIRC2) instrument, in the K, H, or J passbands. MOA-2013-BLG-220 was first observed
in 2015 with the NIRC2 laser guide adaptive optics system, using the wide camera in the K passband
(λc ∼ 2.1μm). Adaptive optics capabilities are crucial for ground-based observations, as it accounts
for the distortion effects due to the Earth’s atmosphere. In 2019, additional data was taken with the
narrow NIRC2’s narrow camera in the K passband.
