chunks.heading: Abstract
chunks.text:
Astronomy & Astrophysics manuscript no. aa61606-26 ©ESO 2026
October 12, 2026
The origin of the large heavy element contents of warm Jupiters
Bertram Bitsch
Department of Physics, University College Cork, Cork, T12 R229, Ireland
October 12, 2026
ABSTRACT
Planet interior models have revealed that warm Jupiters should harbor large heavy element masses, where Jupiter mass planets could
consist of up to 30-40% of heavy elements (heavier than hydrogen and helium). At the same time, it is unclear if the heavy element
mass of giant planets decreases with decreasing stellar masses. Within the pebble drift and evaporation scenario, inward drifting
pebbles can evaporate and enrich the inner disc with vapor to super-stellar values, which can then be accreted by growing giant
planets. Due to a sequential evaporation sequence, where H2O evaporates in the inner disc, while CO2, CH4 and CO evaporate in the
outer disc, the enrichment of the disc with vapor decreases with increasing orbital distance. We employ the chemcomp code to model
the migration and growth of planets via pebble and gas accretion in discs around stars with different masses and discs with different
sizes. Our simulations show (i) that pebble drift and evaporation can explain the wide range of derived heavy element contents of
giant planets. (ii) Giant planets forming around stars with larger disc sizes can accrete larger quantities of heavy elements, because
these discs can maintain a high pebble flux for a longer time, allowing the inner discs to be enriched for longer, resulting in planets
with a higher heavy element content. (iii) Planets forming or migrating interior to the water ice line can accrete larger amounts of
heavy elements via the accretion of vapor enriched gas compared to planets forming in the outer disc regions. (iv) Metal rich stars
can allow the formation of planets that are more enriched in heavy elements, if they form in the inner disc regions. Planets forming
in the outer disc regions will be - independently of the disc metallicity - much less enriched compared to their counterparts that form
in the inner disc and accrete gas enriched with vapor. (v) Planets forming in discs with the same size and total mass, but around stars
with higher mass, are only marginally more enriched compared to their counterparts forming around lower mass star. Put together,
our study suggests that the trend of increasing total heavy element mass with increasing planetary mass is caused by the accretion
of vapor enriched gas in discs with different sizes in the combination with different origins of warm giant planets from the inner and
outer disc.
Key words. accretion discs – planets and satellites: formation – protoplanetary discs – planet and satellites: composition

chunks.heading: 1. Introduction
chunks.text:
The first detection of a planet around a main sequence star re-
vealed a new class of planets: hot Jupiters (Mayor & Queloz
1995). Since this detection many more hot and warm Jupiters
have been found and we are now in an era where we can char-
acterize these planets in much more detail. While we can deter-
mine the atmospheres composition through observations from
the ground (e.g. Pelletier et al. 2021; Prinoth et al. 2024) and
from space (e.g. Ahrer et al. 2023; August et al. 2023; Evans-
Soma et al. 2025), we can also determine with the help of inte-
rior models what the total heavy element budget of these planets
could be (e.g. Thorngren et al. 2016; Bloot et al. 2023; Müller &
Helled 2025; Chachan et al. 2025).
Surprisingly, these warm Jupiters can feature very large
heavy element contents, e.g. 50-60 Earth masses on average for
a Jupiter mass planets (e.g. Thorngren et al. 2016; Bloot et al.
2023; Müller & Helled 2025; Chachan et al. 2025), which could
even be bit higher compared to the highest estimates of our
own Jupiter (e.g. Wahl et al. 2017; Vazan et al. 2018; Helled
et al. 2022; Howard et al. 2023). These studies also indicate that
the average heavy element content of the planets increases with
planetary mass. Furthermore, Peerani et al. (2026a) showed that
this trend also holds when using different assumptions for the in-
Send offprint requests to: B. Bitsch,
e-mail: bbitsch@ucc.ie
terior structure (e.g. 2 layer core and envelope, fully convective,
dilute core), showing the robustness of this trend.
Recently an additional trend has emerged: Müller & Helled
(2025) showed that warm Jupiters around M-dwarfs could be
less enriched in heavy elements than their equal mass counter-
parts around FGK-type stars. Considering that a certain amount
of heavy elements is necessary to form the planets in the first
place, it is surprising that the overall enrichment of these planets
around M-dwarfs is lower. However, this trend was not recov-
ered in the study by Chachan et al. (2025), opening the question
if the heavy element mass of giant planets is really a function of
stellar mass.
As it is well known that stars that are enriched in heavy el-
ements host Jupiters more frequently (e.g. Santos et al. 2004;
Fischer & Valenti 2005; Johnson et al. 2010), due to the more ef-
ficient formation of planetesimals and planets, one could specu-
late that warm Jupiters forming around metal rich stars should be
more metal rich as well (as they could accrete more of the plan-
etesimals and other solids). However, the observations of Teske
et al. (2019) do not support this statement. They show instead
that there is no real correlation between the heavy element mass
fraction of warm Jupiters forming around metal rich stars com-
pared to their counterparts forming around metal poorer stars.
The origin of these large heavy element contents is still not
entirely known even though different models exist. One sets of
models focuses on the accretion of large amount of planetesimals
during migration (e.g. Shibata et al. 2020; Knierim et al. 2022),
Article number, page 1 of 18
arXiv:2610.13762v1 [astro-ph.EP] 9 Oct 2026
-- 1 of 18 --
A&A proofs: manuscript no. aa61606-26
while other models focus on giant impacts between the planets
(e.g. Ginzburg & Chiang 2020). Alternatively, the planet could
also be enriched by the accretion of gas enriched with volatile
vapor (e.g. Booth et al. 2017; Schneider & Bitsch 2021; Bitsch
et al. 2022) or small dust grains that are accreted with the gas
(e.g. Morbidelli et al. 2023; Bitsch & Mah 2023).
This alternative scenario to explain the formation of these
heavily enriched giant planets relates back to the disc evolu-
tion. As mm-cm sized particles - so called pebbles - form in the
disc, they start to drift inwards efficiently (e.g. Weidenschilling
1977; Brauer et al. 2008). As these pebbles cross evaporation
fronts (e.g. Öberg et al. 2011) they can release their volatiles into
the gas phase (e.g. Piso et al. 2015; Booth et al. 2017; Schnei-
der & Bitsch 2021; Mah et al. 2023). As the gas moves much
slower than the pebbles, large levels of enrichment with vapor
(e.g. H2O, CO2, CO) can be achieved (e.g. Schneider & Bitsch
2021; Kalyaan et al. 2021; Mah et al. 2023). Observations of pro-
toplanetary discs confirm these large vapor enrichments in the
inner disc regions (e.g. Banzatti et al. 2023; Perotti et al. 2023;
Colmenares et al. 2024).
Observations of discs around M-dwarfs showed that the in-
ner regions of these discs are enriched with carbon bearing
species, in contrast to solar type stars, where water is domi-
nant (e.g. Pascucci et al. 2013; Banzatti et al. 2023; Colmenares
et al. 2024). This trend can be explained as well by pebble drift
and evaporation (Mah et al. 2023): as the disc around M-dwarfs
are colder, the evaporation fronts of the major volatile carriers
(e.g. H2O, CO2, CH4, CO) are closer to their central star. Conse-
quently, the released volatiles take less time to be accreted onto
the central star, due to the shorter viscous timescale. As the wa-
ter ice line is very close to the central star for M-dwarfs, the wa-
ter vapor is significantly depleted within 1-2 Myr and replaced
by carbon rich vapor moving inwards from the outer disc. In
contrast, this process can take even more than 10 Myr for solar
type stars. This implies that the total vapor fraction in the in-
ner disc regions could be larger for solar type stars compared to
M-dwarfs1.
Planets forming in the inner disc regions around solar type
stars can thus accrete large amounts of vapor, explaining their
large heavy element enrichment (Booth et al. 2017; Schneider &
Bitsch 2021; Bitsch et al. 2022; Ohno et al. 2026; Balogh et al.
2026). While the trend that planets accreting interior to the wa-
ter ice line harbor larger heavy element contents (e.g. Schneider
& Bitsch 2021; Ohno et al. 2026) and that planetesimal forma-
tion and accretion results in lower heavy element contents (e.g.
Danti et al. 2023; Balogh et al. 2026) seems well established, it
is unclear how these trends scale with the disc properties. In par-
ticular, it is unclear what exact role the disc size, the disc mass,
the disc’s viscosity, the disc’s metallicity as well as the stellar
mass play.
In this work, we employ the disc evolution and planet for-
mation code chemcomp (Schneider & Bitsch 2021) to study the
evolution of the vapor content in protoplanetary discs and how
this evolution affects the total heavy element content of plan-
ets growing around stars with different masses and different disc
sizes. Our work is structured as follows. In section 2 we dis-
cuss our methodology and show in section 3 how pebble drift
and evaporation enriches inner discs around stars with different
masses and sizes. In section 4 we discuss the heavy element con-
tent of individual planets, while we show the results for a general
1 The study by Mah et al. (2023) assumes that the disc size increases
with the stellar mass, allow discs around higher mass stars to maintain
their pebble flux for a longer time.
population in section 5. We the discuss the shortcomings and the
implications of our work in section 6 and close with the conclu-
sion in section 7.
2. Methods
We use the disc evolution and planet formation code chemcomp
(Schneider & Bitsch 2021) to study how inward drifting peb-
bles evaporate and enrich the disc with vapor and how much of
the vapor is accreted onto forming planets. The code contains a
viscous disc evolution model combined with pebble growth and
drift, following the approach outlined in Birnstiel et al. (2012),
where we also trace different chemical elements within the disc
and inside forming planets (see table 1). We use a solar com-
position (Asplund et al. 2009) for all our simulations, but vary
the total metallicity for different simulations. The chemical ele-
ments are distributed into different solids (see table 2). We note
that the amount of water is strongly influenced by the amount
of CO, CO2, and rocky materials, as only the leftover oxygen is
forming water. In our model we use 60% of carbon in refractory
carbon grains.
Our model does not take the temperature evolution of the
disc into account, due to simplicity. The temperature structure of
the disc is calculated as the balance between viscous and stel-
lar heating as well as radiative cooling at the beginning of the
simulations and remains at the same level throughout the simu-
lation. The position of the evaporation fronts is thus determined
by the stellar luminosity, as well as by the disc mass and size
which set the viscous heating. However, we expect that this does
not affect the general conclusions of our study, as vapor enriched
gas would still exist interior to the inwards moving evaporation
fronts and we place our results in relation to evaporation fronts
rather than orbital distances.
The planets in our models grow first via pebble accretion
(Johansen & Lambrechts 2017), which stops at the pebble iso-
lation mass, when the planet opens a partial gap (Lambrechts
et al. 2014; Bitsch et al. 2018). This is then followed by a
slow gas contraction phase that leads into runaway gas accretion
(Ndugu et al. 2021). The contraction phase of the envelope de-
pends strongly on the planetary core mass, but also on the opac-
ity within the envelope, regulated by the dust grains and their
opacity (e.g. Ikoma et al. 2000; Bitsch & Savvidou 2021). De-
pending on the assumed envelope opacity, also relatively small
mass cores could transition into runaway accretion. Here we use
an envelope opacity of 0.05cm2/g as in our previous simulations
(e.g. Schneider & Bitsch 2021), which allows cores of ≈3 Earth
masses to already transition into runaway accretion2 (see also
Peerani et al. 2026b). During their growth the planets can mi-
grate in type-I (Paardekooper et al. 2011) and type-II migration
(Baruteau et al. 2014). We additionally take the effects of the
heating (Benítez-Llambay et al. 2015) and dynamical torques
(Paardekooper 2014) into account that can allow outward migra-
tion of planets even at low viscosities (e.g. Baumann & Bitsch
2020). The model is explained in detail in Schneider & Bitsch
(2021).

that the metallicity is the same, independently of the stellar type,
as motivated by observations (e.g. Souto et al. 2022). We as-

The here adopted disc sizes are on the larger side, where mm-
observations of class II discs indicate mean sizes smaller than 50
AU (e.g. Hendler et al. 2020), whereas the CO disc radius can be
a factor of a few larger (e.g. Long et al. 2022). The positions
of our CO evaporation fronts are in line with these constraints.
In addition, class II discs are already evolved and planet forma-
tion might have already happened (Savvidou & Bitsch 2025) and
the mm-disc sizes have reduced in time (e.g. Appelgren et al.
2023, 2025). As the most massive discs are more efficient to
form giant planets (Savvidou & Bitsch 2023), we can focus our
study on these objects. As the occurrence rate of giant planets is
only around 10-15% (e.g. Johnson et al. 2010; Wittenmyer et al.
2020), we can make the assumption that giant planets form in the
more massive and also larger discs. Observationally, discs with
mm-sizes above 100-150 AU exist (e.g. Andrews et al. 2018a;
Huang et al. 2018; Tobin et al. 2020) and we thus focus on disc
with these sizes.
We use a constant grain fragmentation velocity of 5m/s, in
agreement with our previous studies (Mah et al. 2023). Guzmán
Franco et al. (2026) showed that the influence of the grain frag-
mentation velocity on the planetary heavy element content is not
very large. In contrast, Guzmán Franco et al. (2026) showed that
the heavy element content of giant planets depends crucially on
the disc’s viscosity and the initial starting position of the plan-
ets. We thus use three different α viscosity values (see table 3)
and probe 25 different initial planetary positions for all stellar
masses and viscosities. This allows us to capture planets that
form in different disc regions and will also stay exterior to the
water evaporation front, interior to which the heavy element con-
tent is largest due to evaporation of inward drifting water ice rich
pebbles (Schneider & Bitsch 2021; Mah et al. 2024).
We compare the heavy element mass fraction of the planets
formed in our simulations with the heavy element mass fraction
derived from interior models of planets with precise mass and
radius measurements (Thorngren et al. 2016; Bloot et al. 2023;
Müller & Helled 2025; Chachan et al. 2025). While many au-
thors have derived scaling laws of the heavy element content of
planets with the planetary mass, they all show the trend that the
heavy element mass increases with planetary mass. The trend of
increasing heavy element mass with planetary mass holds also
for different assumed interior structures of the planet (Peerani
et al. 2026a). Here we chose to mainly compare our simulations
to the scaling found in Chachan et al. (2025), because of their
larger observational sample.
3. Disc enrichment
As planets grow from material inside their natal protoplanetary
discs, we first investigate how the heavy element content in the
vapor phase evolves in discs around stars with different masses.
We thus show in Fig. 1 the vapor fraction in the gas phase, con-
sisting of the summation of the volatile species up to an evap-

meaning FeS does not contribute to the vapor fraction3.

various evaporation fronts (at e.g. 1.0 Myr). As time progresses
further, basically all pebbles have drifted inwards, leading to a

Fig. 1, however, reveals another trend in line with the re-
sults of Mah et al. (2023): the vapor enrichment interior to the
water ice line lasts shorter in discs with smaller sizes. This is
evolution is caused by two slightly competing effects. Disc with
smaller sizes (but with the same total mass) harbor a higher sur-
face density and are thus hotter compared to discs with larger
sizes. Consequently, the inner evaporation fronts (carbon grains,
water, NH3 and H2O) are slightly farther from the central star.
On the other hand, the larger discs can sustain a large pebble flux
for a longer time, because the small micrometer sized dust grains
take longer to grow in the outer disc regions. Once the pebble
flux decays, the overall vapor enrichment decreases, because the
influx of volatile rich material is stopped. As this happens earlier
in the small discs, their vapor content decreases faster compared
to the discs with large sizes. While the initial vapor enrichment
can easily be a few 10% of the total amount of gas, it essen-
tially reduces to the stellar value in a few Myrs around discs
of small sizes. In contrast, the vapor can stay around for longer
times around discs with sizes of 100 AU and above. In this case,
the vapor fraction can remain at a level of ∼10-20% even at 5
Myr.
The duration of the vapor enrichment in the inner disc re-
gions is also related to the viscous evolution of the disc, because
the viscosity determines how long the vapor released from the
inward drifting pebbles can remain in the disc. We show in Ap-
pendix A the vapor evolution of protoplanetary discs with vary-
ing stellar mass, disc sizes and viscosities. The reported trend,
that discs with larger sizes can support a larger vapor enrich-
ment for a longer time remains. However, at higher viscosity, the
faster viscous evolution in combination with the smaller pebble
sizes due to the fragmentation limited regime (see Birnstiel et al.
(2012)), result in a faster depletion of the inner disc’s vapor con-
tent.
Our simulations thus clearly show that the enrichment of in-
ner discs with vapor is a strong function with disc size, in agree-
ment with our previous simulations (Mah et al. 2023). However,
recent observations with the JWST show tentative evidence that
the inner disc water content might instead be anti-correlated with
the disc size and that smaller discs show a larger water content
(e.g. Banzatti et al. 2020, 2023; Gasman et al. 2025). In contrast,
Krijt et al. (2025) find a correlation between the water line flux
and the location of the innermost dust gap detected with ALMA
observations, hinting that the inner disc water content might not
be influenced by the disc size, but instead by pebble traps in the
disc, shown also by models (e.g. Kalyaan et al. 2023; Mah et al.
2024; Easterwood et al. 2024). While outer gaps might block a
fraction of the pebbles, their influence on the inner disc compo-
sition depends strongly on their depth as well as at what stage of
the disc evolution they appear.
We will now investigate how this effect influences the heavy
element content within giant planets in discs without outer gaps,
to allow to probe the maximal heavy element content giant plan-
ets can achieve within this scenario. We discuss the influence of
outer gaps in appendix B.

content of individual planets before discussing population level
trends in section 5. In our work, we define the heavy element
mass of the planet as the sum of heavy elements in the core and
in the atmosphere.

4.1. Influence of the planetary position
We show in Fig. 2 the growth tracks of planets forming at seven
different orbital distances up to 5 AU in discs with α = 10−4
around a 1.4 M⊙ star. The planets first start by accreting inward
drifting pebbles until they have reached their pebble isolation
mass. During this growth process, the planet only contains very
little amounts of hydrogen (mostly due to the accretion of water
ice), resulting in a heavy element mass that is basically equal to
the total planetary mass.
Once the planet starts to accrete gas, which consists out of
hydrogen and helium, but also to a large fraction of heavy el-
ements (see Fig. A.1), the planetary heavy element content re-
duces by different values, depending on the planetary position.
The planets forming interior to the water ice line see a very con-
sistent steep increase of their heavy element content with plane-
tary mass due to efficient accretion of water vapor. As these plan-
ets migrate even across the carbon grain evaporation front, their
heavy element content increases further. These planets basically
always show a heavy element content larger than the average
heavy element content derived from interior models of Chachan
et al. (2025) once they reach around 0.3 Jupiter masses.
The planets forming exterior to the water ice line do only
accrete very little amounts of vapor with the gas (e.g. CO2), re-
sulting in a first nearly horizontal evolution in the heavy element
- planetary mass diagram after they have reached pebble isola-
tion mass. However, once these planets cross interior to the water
evaporation front, their heavy element content increases signif-
icantly. This very rapid increase of the heavy element fraction
of these planets is also aided by the ability of the planet to trap
pebbles: As the planet reaches its pebble isolation mass, it will
trap a large amount of pebbles exterior to its orbit. As the planet
migrates inwards, these pebbles follow and will eventually re-
lease their volatiles into the gas phase when the planet crosses
an evaporation front. This will lead to a burst of vapor in the
inner disc (see Eberlein et al. 2024) and thus allow the planet to
accrete large amounts of vapor, significantly increasing its heavy
element mass.
We note that planetesimal formation in the pressure perturba-
tions generated by the planets would decrease the available peb-
ble mass to evaporate, resulting in less enrichment of the planets
migrating into the inner disc regions. However, not all pebbles
are transformed into planetesimals, and mm observations indi-
cate that these rings could contain up to 100 Earth mass of peb-
bles (Dullemond et al. 2018), in line with our simulations. If
the formation of planetesimals in the outer disc were efficient, it
would increase the difference in the heavy element mass between
planets forming in the inner and outer disc regions.
Consequently, the heavy element content of the planets
shows a trend with orbital distance. Planets forming completely
exterior to the water ice line show a reduced heavy element con-
tent4 compared to planets accreting gas interior to the water ice
line (see also Booth et al. 2017; Schneider & Bitsch 2021; Ohno
et al. 2026).

5. Planetary population
We analyse in this section the general outcome of our large set
of simulations (see table 3). Generally, planets forming in discs
with larger viscosities will grow to larger masses due to the
larger disc accretion rate that sets the planetary gas accretion
rate. We note that a shorter disc lifetime would result in less
massive planets (see Appendix C).
5.1. General trends
We show in Fig. 5 the final heavy element mass as well as
the metallicity of the planets divided by the stellar metallicity
(Z=0.016) from all our simulations. The different colors corre-

Fig. 5 verifies the trend of the previous discussed heavy

Planets forming around stars with larger disc sizes can cover

The formation of planets above 2-3 Jupiter masses, requires

5.2. Origin of the heavy element content
Fig. 1 shows that the vapor content in the gas phase increases to-
wards the inner disc, especially around the water ice line, where
planets migrating across the water ice line should harbor large
heavy element contents (Fig. 2). We show in Fig. 6 the heavy
element mass and the Zplanet/Z⋆ ratios of the planets as function
of their total mass and final orbital position color coded by their
relative position to the water ice line. As the position of the wa-
ter ice line is a strong function of the stellar mass and the disc’s
viscosity (e.g. Fig. A.1 and Fig. A.2), we use the position rel-
ative to the water ice line rather than absolute distances in AU.
We remind the reader that the temperature structure of our disc
does not evolve in time.
Fig. 6 shows a very clear trend of the total heavy element
mass of the planets as function of their distance to the water ice
line. All planets with more than ∼50 Earth masses of heavy ele-
ments have either formed completely or migrated interior to the
water ice line. In contrast, planets below ∼50 Earth masses could
stay exterior to the water ice line, but could have also migrated
interior to it. The inward migrating planets with these low heavy
element masses formed predominantly around stars with small
disc sizes and in discs with high viscosity. Both - small disc sizes
and high viscosities - reduce the vapor mass fraction in the inner
disc (Fig. A.1 and Fig. A.2), leading to the formation of planets
with a smaller heavy element content. The here found trend that
planets with large heavy element content have accreted gas in-
terior to the water ice line is similar to the study of Ohno et al.
(2026), but our study shows that also planets interior to the water
ice line could have small heavy element contents. In reverse, our
study shows that planets forming exterior to the water ice line
will not have a large heavy element content.
The Zplanet/Z⋆ ratio reflects this trend as well. Giant planets
with a Zplanet/Z⋆ ratio larger than ≈5 have migrated into the inner
disc and accreted large amounts of vapor. In contrast, planets
with a Zplanet/Z⋆ ratio lower than 5, could have either formed
completely exterior to the water ice line, or migrated across the
water ice line if they formed around low mass stars or in high
viscosity environments.
We note that the planets following the 0% H/He line or show-
ing a Zplanet/Z⋆ ratio of around 60, are planets that did not start
gas accretion efficiently. These planets are dominated by their
core and only show very little hydrogen (due to the accretion
of water ice into their core), independently of their final orbital
position.
We note that basically all planets have a heavy element frac-
tion that is larger than the stellar value. This is caused by the
formation of the planetary core, which can contain already a few
Earth masses of heavy elements, independently how efficient va-
por accretion is. Consequently, these planets show total heavy
element contents below the mean value derived in Chachan et al.
(2025).
5.3. Trends with stellar metallicity
Our standard simulations use Z=0.016, which corresponds to the
solar metallicity (table 1). In order to probe how a change in
metallicity of the host star would change the planetary heavy el-
ement content, we probe a slightly higher and a slightly lower
metallicity as well, corresponding to Z=0.010 and Z=0.024, re-
spectively. In the bracket notation, these changes correspond to
[Z/H] = +0.2 , [Z/H] = −0.2 .
The heavy element content of the planets formed in the inner
disc scales roughly with the overall metallicity, as most of the
C, O, and N has evaporated. The planets can then proportionally
accrete more vapor and we expect that planets forming in high
metallicity environments in the inner regions should be more en-
riched in heavy elements. Fig. 7 confirms this trend. However we
observe also a trend with orbital distance, where planets forming
further out in the disc are less affected by an increase of the stel-
lar metallicity.
The left hand side of Fig. 7 shows the evolution of the plan-
etary heavy element mass as function of the planetary mass. The
planets forming in the discs with higher heavy element content
feature a slightly larger heavy element content compared to the
planets forming in the disc with lower metallicity, independent
of the stellar mass and disc size. This is caused by the initial
formation location of the planets at 2.0 AU, interior to the CO2
evaporation front, where already some vapor can be accreted.
However, as soon as the planets migrate across the water ice
line, the larger disc metallicity results in much larger heavy el-
ement masses of the planets. In contrast, the planets forming at
20 AU stay always exterior to the CO2 evaporation front and
thus also exterior to the water evaporation front and their heavy
element mass is determined basically by their core mass alone.
As the pebble isolation mass is independent of the disc metallic-
ity, the planets essentially feature the same heavy element mass
independently of their birth metallicity environment. The small
differences in the heavy element mass are explained by the ac-
cretion of a slightly larger fraction of CO and nitrogen rich gas
around the higher metallicity stars.
The right hand side of Fig. 7 shows the heavy element mass
of planets formed around a 1.4 M⊙ star in discs with three dif-
ferent metallicities and α = 10−4 as function of their final orbital
position. The planets start up to 20 AU and slowly migrate in-
wards during their evolution. Fig. 7 reveals 3 different distinct re-
gions in respect to the final heavy element content of the formed
planets.
Exterior to the CO2 evaporation front, the disc’s vapor con-
tent is very small, because CO and CH4 vapor are very inefficient
in moving inwards (Fig. 1) and also contain only a small amount
of carbon and oxygen. The heavy element mass of the planets
is thus determined mostly by their core mass, set by the pebble
isolation mass, with a small addition from the CO, CH4 and N2
that was present in the gas phase of the disc. As the pebble iso-
lation mass is independent of the disc’s metallicity (e.g. Bitsch
et al. 2018), there is no difference in the heavy element mass of

6. Discussion
We discuss in this section the implications of our work as well as
some shortcomings of our model that could be improved in the
future.
6.1. Shortcomings of our model
The heavy element content of our model is driven by the ac-
cretion of vapor in the inner disc regions. Planets forming in
the outer disc regions are dominated by the core mass, set by
the pebble isolation mass (Lambrechts et al. 2014; Bitsch et al.
2018). Our model thus ignores the formation and accretion of
planetesimals as well as of collisions between the planets them-
selves. However, Danti et al. (2023) showed that the formation
of planetesimals in discs decreases the vapor content in the gas
phase and consequently the heavy element content of forming
planets. Including the accretion of the formed planetesimals re-
sulted in a relatively low heavy element fraction, because the
planetesimal to gas ratio in the discs is lower than the vapor con-
tent (Danti et al. 2023), as also found by Balogh et al. (2026).
Furthermore, the accretion of planetesimals is not 100% effi-
cient, whereas the accretion of gas enriched with vapor will oc-
cur at the corresponding mass fraction of the vapor within the
disc. Shibata et al. (2020) used N-body simulations to study how
many planetesimals could be accreted onto migrating giant plan-
ets. However, their model failed to produce heavy element con-
tents above 100 Earth masses, which are a typical outcome in our
simulations. In our study we are mostly interested in the maxi-
mum heavy element content the planets could harbor, which is
why out study is restricted to a pure pebble accretion scenario.
Ginzburg & Chiang (2020) used collisions between giant
planets with massive cores (up to 30 Earth mass cores) to explain
the heavy element content of giant planets. While their model
could eventually produce these large heavy element fractions un-
der the assumptions that a lot of gas is lost during the collisions,
they did not model the collision via N-body interactions, which
normally show less frequent collisions (e.g. Beaugé & Nesvorný
2012; Bitsch & Izidoro 2023) of these objects. Furthermore, the
formation of many Jupiter type planets in the inner disc is not
reproduced in N-body simulations (Poon et al. 2021). Chachan
et al. (2025) also used a simple estimate via planetary collisions
to explain the heavy element masses of giant planets. They con-
cluded that collisions between planets can not explain the Jupiter
mass planets that feature heavy element contents above 50ish
Earth masses. However, collisions might be needed to explain
planets below ∼40 Earth masses, that have heavy element mass
fractions of close to 100%. Our model has difficulties produc-
ing these type of planets, which would be essentially planets that
have just reached the pebble isolation mass, but never accreted
gas (see also appendix C).
Our chemical partitioning model shows that roughly 75% of
the heavy element fraction is made up of O, C, and N. These
elements are highly volatile and exist predominantly in the gas
phase and can thus be accreted efficiently with the gas onto the
planet. However, some of the oxygen is hidden in the refractory
solids, so that at t=0, roughly 60% of the heavy elements are in a
gaseous form in the inner disc regions. If accretion thus proceeds
only via planetesimals (which is not 100% efficient as well), a
large fraction of heavy elements will not be accreted, resulting
in a lower heavy element enrichment of the planets (see Danti
et al. 2023)
The chemical partitioning model (table 2) assumes that 60%
of the carbon is within refractory carbon grains. However, if a
lower fraction of carbon were in carbon grains, and instead the
fraction of CO and CO2 would be larger, the partitioning model
would predict less water, because more oxygen is stored in CO
and CO2 (Bitsch & Battistini 2020). Consequently, the inner disc
would be less enriched in water and carbon vapor, resulting in
less enriched planets. Schneider & Bitsch (2021) used a par-
titioning model without carbon grains and consequently found
that planets are less enriched by vapor compared to our study
here. The water content would also be influenced by the stellar
C/O ratio (Bitsch & Battistini 2020; Cabral et al. 2023), showing
the importance to use detailed stellar abundances if the formation
of individual systems is explained (O’Donovan & Bitsch 2026).
Our model assumes a smooth disc that allows efficient in-
ward drift of pebbles that can thus enrich the inner disc regions.
However, outer pressure perturbations could hinder the inward
drift of pebbles (e.g. Pinilla et al. 2012; Kalyaan et al. 2023;
Mah et al. 2024; Luo et al. 2026). Depending on the timing,
the strength of the perturbation and the disc’s viscosity, pebbles
could be blocked efficiently, resulting in a decrease of the inward
drifting pebbles and consequently to less enrichment of vapor in
the inner disc (e.g. Kalyaan et al. 2023; Mah et al. 2024). If pres-
sure perturbations would be efficient in the early stages of disc
evolution, our model predicts a lower heavy element mass frac-
tion. However, if the outer pressure perturbations were present
from the beginning of the disc evolution, giant planet formation
would also be quenched, as the pebble flux would be reduced
significantly (Lambrechts et al. 2019). We show the evolution of
the planetary heavy element content in discs with outer gaps in
appendix B.
Models with multiple forming planets also show that the en-
richment of inner planets is not altered significantly by the outer
gap opening planets, if the planets form in sequential order from
inside out (Eberlein et al. 2024). On the other hand, very young
disc do not show any sign of substructure (e.g. Zormpas et al.
2022), indicating that at least initially large amounts of pebbles
could make their way into the inner disc, causing the enrichment
needed to form giant planets with large heavy element contents.
These large vapor enrichments are also observed in discs with
gap and ring like structure (e.g. Banzatti et al. 2023), indicating
that vapor accretion will play a role in shaping the giant planet
population.
Our simulations are agnostic about the disc sizes as function
of stellar mass. However, if the disc size were to decrease with
decreasing stellar mass (e.g. Andrews et al. 2010), our simula-
tions would predict that giant planets around lower mass stars
should be less enriched in heavy elements compared to planets
forming around higher mass stars. This would be in line with the
trend of Müller & Helled (2025), see appendix E. On the other
hand, the observational trend of disc size with stellar mass seems
to point towards the fact that disc sizes do not strongly depend
on the stellar mass (e.g. Hendler et al. 2020; Long et al. 2022),
showing the importance of combining constraints from exoplan-
ets and protoplanetary discs to understand planet formation.
6.2. Implications for giant planet formation
The large heavy element content of giant planets has been used
to infer their formation location (O’Donovan & Bitsch 2026).
However, such studies require the detailed stellar abundances as
input in order to constrain the heavy element content during the
gas disc phase. Here we extend the simulations to also under-
stand the heavy element content of giant planets around different
stellar types.

The analysis of (Müller & Helled 2025) revealed that giant
planets forming around M-dwarfs should harbor a smaller heavy
element content compared to planets of the same total mass
around FGK stars. In particular they find that the giant plan-
ets around M-dwarfs harbour a maximum of 50 Earth masses
of heavy elements with a mean closer to 20 Earth masses. In
contrast, the planets around FGK type stars in their sample can
have heavy element masses above 100 Earth masses. However,
the study by Chachan et al. (2025) does not recover this trend.
Our simulations also only show a very small dependency of the
stellar mass on the heavy element content of forming giant plan-
ets (Fig. 4), in line with the observational trend of Chachan et al.
(2025).
Our simulations predict that giant planets with large heavy
element contents (e.g. above the fit of Chachan et al. 2025) mi-
grated inwards across the water ice line and should thus have
obliquities and eccentricities close to zero. In contrast, planets
with a low heavy element content could have formed exterior to
the water ice line. This implies that scattering events would be
needed to bring these planets to their currently observed orbits.
Thus our simulations predict that planets with lower heavy ele-
ment contents are more likely to have significant obliquities or
are on an eccentric orbit compared to planets with a high heavy
element content. Put together, our simulations suggest that metal
rich planets form via disc migration, while metal poor warm gi-
ant planets either experienced scattering events or migrated in-
wards in high viscosity environments.
Metal rich stars are more prone to host giant planets (e.g.
Santos et al. 2004; Fischer & Valenti 2005; Johnson et al. 2010).
Naturally, our model predicts that planets forming around more
metal rich stars to be more metal rich, if they form within the
same evaporation fronts (Fig. 7). However, the observations from
Teske et al. (2019) indicate that more metal rich stars do not, on
average, make more metal rich planets. Within our simulations
this observation can be explained naturally by different forma-
tion locations. If planets form exterior to the water ice line, even
around metal rich stars, they will feature a lower heavy element
mass compared to planets forming interior to the water ice line,
even if the star is metal poorer. In particular, we find that the
heavy element mass of planets can increase by a factor of 10
from exterior to interior to the water ice line, while the heavy
element content seems to scale just linearly with host star metal-
licity (Fig. 7). Planet formation itself, on the other hand, is more
efficient at larger orbital distances around metal rich stars (e.g.
Bitsch et al. 2015; Emsenhuber et al. 2021), leading naturally to
the large variety of heavy element masses of giant planets form-
ing around more metal rich stars.
In our model, the inward migrating planets feature an inter-
esting phase during their formation: as the planets migrate into
regions with larger and larger vapor contents, the heavy element
content in the planetary atmosphere will increase as a function
of planetary radius (under the assumption that there is no mix-
ing). This could have potential implications for the observations
of planetary atmospheres and how these link to the bulk abun-
dances (see Knierim & Helled 2024).
Recently, Lee et al. (2026) pointed to the potential prob-
lem that the large fraction of free floating planets should contain
more heavy elements compared to what is available during the
disc stage. However, their estimates of the heavy element masses
is based on the fit provided by Thorngren et al. (2016), who
suggested that a Jupiter mass planet, on average, should have
58 Earth masses of heavy elements. However, the free floating
planet population might originate from the outer disc regions,
where the heavy element content of the planets is smaller by a
factor of a few. Consequently, there could be no issue with the
overall mass budget (see also Savvidou & Bitsch 2025).
Within our solar system, Jupiter’s heavy element content is
derived through complex interior models (e.g. Wahl et al. 2017;
Vazan et al. 2018; Helled et al. 2022). Current estimates place
Jupiter’s core in the range of up to 10 Earth masses, while its total
heavy element content is around 30-50 Earth masses. Within our
model this implies a formation of Jupiter exterior to the water ice
evaporation front. This implies that Jupiter, even if it migrated
several AU (Walsh et al. 2011), did not cross the water ice line
in this process.
Our simulations show that small (R0 = 50 AU) discs around
solar mass stars can form objects in the brown dwarf mass
regime, defined here as 13 Jupiter masses (e.g. Fig 3). These ob-
jects then harbor super-stellar atmospheric abundances (Fig. 5,
Fig. D.1). In contrast, observations seems to indicate that close-
in brown dwarfs might favor metallicities corresponding to their
host star (e.g. Xuan et al. 2024). We note that our model can also
produce brown dwarfs with sub-stellar metallciities, but these
objects would have then brought close towards their host star via
scattering mechanisms. We thus think that the bulk metallicity
in combination with the atmospheric abundances could indicate
if close-in brown dwarfs formed via the same formation chan-
nels as giant planet or if they exhibit a preference for scattering
events.

chunks.heading: 7. Summary and conclusion
chunks.text:
In this work we have studied the origin of the heavy element
content of giant planets. We use the chemcomp code (Schneider
& Bitsch 2021), which includes pebble drift and evaporation, as
well as planetary growth via pebble and gas accretion. Due to
the velocity difference between pebbles and gas, the inner disc
can be enriched with vapor originating from evaporating peb-
bles to largely super-stellar values (Fig. 1). As the planets grow
and migrate through the disc, they can accrete this vapor and
consequently accrete large amounts of heavy elements (see also
Schneider & Bitsch 2021; Ohno et al. 2026). In our study, we
do not take the formation and accretion of planetesimals into
account, as their formation and accretion would result in lower
total heavy element contents of giant planets (Danti et al. 2023;
Balogh et al. 2026). However, we are here interested in the max-
imal heavy element content the planets could reach. In the same
line of thought, we only model the growth and evolution of single
planets in discs, which thus have access to the full heavy element
content of the disc (even though multiple sequentially forming
planets only minimally influence the heavy element content of
the innermost planet, Eberlein et al. (2024)).
In particular we focus on planets forming in discs with dif-
ferent sizes, masses, and viscosities around stars with different
stellar masses. Discs with larger sizes can retain a larger heavy
element content in their inner regions for longer (Fig. 1), while
the stellar mass only plays a minor role (Fig. A.1). This has con-
sequences for the heavy element content of the gas accreting
planets in these discs. Our main findings are illustrated in Fig. 8
and summarized below:
– Planets forming in the inner regions (interior to the CO2 and
H2O evaporation fronts) around stars with smaller disc con-
tain less heavy elements compared to planets (of the same
total mass) forming around stars with larger discs (Fig. 5).
This is caused by the fact that inner discs can hold on longer
to their vapor enrichment around if the discs are larger. This

– We find that planets forming in discs with the same total
mass and size, but around stars with higher masses, harbor
slightly larger heavy element contents compared to planets
forming around lower mass stars (Fig. 4). This is caused by
the fact that discs around higher mass stars can retain their
heavy element content in the vapor phase for slightly longer
(Fig. A.1 and Fig. 1). Put together, we find a stronger depen-
dency of the planetary heavy element content with the disc
size than the stellar mass.
– Generally, we find that planets harboring a heavy ele-
ment mass above the observationally derived heavy element
masses (e.g Thorngren et al. 2016; Chachan et al. 2025;
Peerani et al. 2026a), need to have migrated interior of the
water evaporation front (Fig. 6). However, planets that have
a lower heavy element mass/content could have migrated in-
ward as well, especially around stars with smaller disc size
(Fig. 5) or in high viscosity environments. Planets accreting
material only exterior to the water ice line, on the other hand,
harbour always heavy element contents below the observa-
tionally derived mean (Fig. 6). This trend becomes particu-
larly clear for the O/H and C/H in the atmosphere (Fig. D.1).
– Metal rich stars can form more metal rich planets, but the
overall heavy element content is determined predominantly
where the planets accrete material within the protoplanetary
disc. If a planet around a metal rich star accretes material
only exterior to the water ice line, it will still be less en-
riched compared to a giant planet forming around a metal
poorer star, as long as that planet accretes most of its mate-
rial interior to the water ice line (Fig. 7). The trend reported
in Teske et al. (2019), namely that more metal rich stars do
not necessarily form more metal rich planets thus implies a
mixture of the origin of giant planets. They either form in or
migrate to the inner disc or form in the outer disc and are then
scattered inwards after the gas-disc phase, implying different
potential obliquities of metal rich vs. metal poor planets.
Our simulations show a complex interplay between stellar
mass, metallicity, disc size, and formation location to explain the
large heavy element contents of giant planets (Fig. 8). Current
observations are limited by small sample sizes making it difficult
to draw a definite conclusion at the moment. We expect that a
combination of stellar metallicity determinations via 4MOST (de
Jong et al. 2012) and planetary detections via PLATO (Rauer
et al. 2014) will help to verify our predictions about the origin
of the large heavy elements mass of giant planets in the coming
years.

Appendix A: Disc compositions
We show in Fig. A.1 the vapor fraction within discs around stars
with different masses. The disc sizes are assumed to scale with
the stellar mass as in Mah et al. (2023) to illustrate the effect of
different stellar masses on the disc evolution and correspond to
the same sizes as in Fig. 1. As smaller stars are less luminous
than their higher mass counter parts, the corresponding evapo-
ration fronts are closer towards the host star. This results in a
slightly faster depletion of the vapor content in the inner discs
around lower mass stars. We emphasise that the faster decrease
of the vapor content is mainly driven by the smaller disc size
(see Fig 1) and the effect of the stellar mass is much smaller (for
the smallest disc size, we find a depletion that is around a factor
of 2-3 faster around the 0.1 Solar mass star compared to the 1.4
Solar mass star). This shows that the vapor content in the disc
primarily depends on the disc size and the effect of the stellar
mass is only a 2nd order effect.
We show in Fig. A.2 the time evolution of the vapor fraction
of discs around stars with different stellar masses and different
disc sizes with α = 10−3. The larger disc viscosity results in a
faster decay of the vapor content in the inner disc. This is caused
by two effects: (i) the larger viscosity limits the size of the peb-
bles in the fragmentation limit (e.g. Birnstiel et al. 2012), result-
ing in reduced radial drift and consequently less enrichment in
the first place and (ii) the larger viscosity allows a faster accre-
tion of the vapor onto the star, depleting the vapor content in the
disc. As for the discs with lower viscosity (Fig. A.1), this ef-
fect is more efficient for lower mass stars with small disc sizes,
where the vapor enrichment can even be lower than the initial va-
por fraction towards the end of the disc’s lifetime. However, the
general trend that inner discs around stars with larger disc sizes
are enriched for a longer time also holds at higher viscosity.
Appendix B: Influence of outer gaps
Outer gaps in protoplanetary discs can block inward flowing
pebbles (e.g. Paardekooper & Mellema 2006; Pinilla et al. 2012),
which will result in less enrichment of vapor in the inner disc re-
gions (e.g. Kalyaan et al. 2023; Mah et al. 2024). The blocking
ability of the gaps depends on their depths as well as when dur-
ing the disc evolution they appear. We include the gap into the
protoplanetary disc via our previous model (Mah et al. 2024).
We introduce the gap profile at a specific time tgap by modi-
fying the α-viscosity parameter in the disc to include a numerical
factor that describes the gap profile.

where 0 ≤ fgap ≤ 1 is the gap depth (lower values mean deeper
gaps), rgap is the location of the gap and σ is the width of the gap

σ = 2Hg(r = rg)/[2 p2 log(2)] . (B.2)

α′ = α/N(r) , (B.3)
where we only apply the modifications via α on the gas surface
density. The original value of α is used for the dust processes.
We show in Fig. B.1 the evolution of the heavy element mass
of planets forming in discs that contain outer gaps at 50 AU.
We introduce gaps with depths of 0.5 and 0.1 either directly at
the beginning of the simulation or after 0.5 Myr. Introducing the
gap at the beginning of the simulations has the biggest effect,
because the planet forming in a disc with a gap depth of 0.1
does not grow very large. This is caused by the fact that the deep
gap blocks inward drifting pebbles efficiently and the planet thus
does not grow. A slightly shallower gap depth allows pebbles
to still drift inwards and thus growth of the planet. However,
the planet grows slower compared to the nominal case and it
thus migrates inwards more efficiently before it transitions into
the gas accretion phase. Consequently, it crosses the water ice
line a bit earlier and starts to accrete water vapor relatively early
during its formation and thus harbors at its early stages a slightly
larger heavy element content compared to the planet forming in
a disc without a gap. However, in the end, the planetary heavy
element content is smaller compared to the planet forming in a
disc without a gap, because the pebble flux into the inner disc is
reduced, reducing the vapor content in the disc as well.
In contrast, if the gap forms at a later time (tgap = 0.5 Myr),
there is not significant effect on the growth of the planetary core,
because the pebbles can flow freely for the first 0.5 Myr. How-
ever, over the course of 5 Myr, some pebbles are blocked and the
heavy element content remains smaller compared to the planet
forming in the simulation without gaps. This shows that outer
gaps can indeed reduce the maximal heavy element content of
planets or even hinders giant planet formation all together, espe-
cially if the gap forms early6. Thus, in order to achieve the max-
imum heavy element content within the pebble drift and evapo-
ration scenario, discs without (initial) gaps are preferred.
Appendix C: Disc lifetime
We show in Fig. C.1 the heavy element mass of planets in discs
whose lifetime is only 2 or 3 Myr. We note that we use the same
simulations as in the main paper, and instead plot the resulting
heavy element masses of the planets after 2 and 3 Myr.
A reduced disc lifetime results in less time for the planet to
accrete gas, giving rise to smaller planetary masses (on average).
This effect allows to fill the parameter space of planets below 0.7
Jupiter masses, where our nominal simulations with a disc life-
time of 5 Myr were not able to produce many planets. This shows
that our model can be applied to the whole mass range of plan-
ets. We note that our simulations allow to reproduce the shape of
the derived heavy element masses as function of planetary mass
of Chachan et al. (2025).
Our simulations also show an empty region between 0%
H/He and 50% H/He fraction. This is caused by the transition
into runaway accretion. Once the planet reaches its pebble isola-
tion mass, it accretes its envelope relatively fast, so that its mass
doubles, but it does not necessarily increase its heavy element
content, which, at this stage, is still dominated by the planetary
core.
Appendix D: Atmospheric abundances
We show in Fig. D.1 the atmospheric O/H, C/H and N/H ratios
for all planets formed in our simulations. The large heavy ele-
ment contents of the giant planets in our simulations originates
from the accretion of vapor enriched gas, visible via the super-
stellar abundance measurements of the volatiles. In particular the
O/H and C/H ratio can reach values larger than 10 times stellar,

simulations form in low viscosity discs, where the vapor con-
tent of the inner disc can remain high during the whole accretion
phase of the planets (Fig. A.1). In contrast, higher mass planets
(above a few Jupiter masses) form in discs with higher viscosi-
ties, leading to a depletion in the vapor content of the disc to-
wards the end of the disc’s lifetime (Fig. A.2), resulting in lower
overall enrichment of these more massive planets. This reflects
the observational trends discussed in Lothringer et al. (2026).
We note that our simulations show that planets can be sub-
stellar in O/H and C/H, if they form in the outer disc regions
and do not accrete large amounts of vapor. However, these plan-
ets, even though they are sub-stellar in their atmospheric abun-
dances have a super-stellar metallicity (Fig. 5), due to the contri-
bution of the planetary core to the overall metallicity. We caution
though to make a direct comparison between our simulations and
the derived observational data, because each planet orbits a star
with different composition that influences the composition of the
growing planets around it (e.g. Bitsch et al. 2022; O’Donovan &

there is no clearly visible trend with N/H. This is caused by the

the different disc sizes.

We show in Fig. E.1 the heavy element evolution of planets

as in discs with different viscosities. The disc sizes are assumed

around lower mass stars harbour a lower heavy element content.

imply from our simulation perspective that the disc size is not
scaling strongly with the stellar mass, as also indicated by obser-

stars have discs with the same sizes, which can thus explain the
diversity of the formed giant planets.

summary.title: The origin of the large heavy element contents of warm Jupiters
summary.executiveSummary:
Planet interior models reveal that warm Jupiters often contain massive heavy element budgets, where a Jupiter-mass planet can consist of up to 30-40% heavy elements (50-60 Earth masses or more of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium). Traditional giant planet formation models relying solely on core accretion or late planetesimal bombardment struggle to explain these enormous heavy element fractions without demanding unphysically high planetesimal capture efficiencies. This study addresses this theoretical gap by investigating how pebble drift and vapor evaporation in protoplanetary disks naturally generate vapor-enriched inner disk regions, which migrating giant planets accrete directly during their growth phase.

Using the detailed chemcomp chemical disk and planet formation code, the paper simulates planetary growth and orbital migration across circumstellar disks of varying sizes, masses, viscosities, and stellar host masses. Inward-drifting pebbles undergo sequential thermal evaporation at critical temperature fronts (such as H2O, CO2, CH4, and CO ice lines), enriching the gas in the inner disk with metal vapor to significantly super-stellar levels. As protoplanets grow through pebble accretion and migrate inward, they accrete this heavily enriched gas, incorporating massive amounts of volatile heavy elements into their envelopes.

The findings establish that disk size, rather than stellar host mass, is the dominant driver of heavy element enrichment in warm Jupiters. Larger protoplanetary disks maintain a prolonged inward flux of drifting pebbles, sustaining elevated gas metallicity in the inner disk for millions of years. This mechanism successfully reproduces the upper limits of heavy element masses inferred from exoplanet interior structures, offering a compelling unified framework for gas giant composition without requiring planetesimal capture.
coreContributions: 1. Demonstrates that pebble drift and thermal evaporation naturally generate super-stellar vapor enrichments in inner protoplanetary disks, providing a robust mechanism to explain the 30-40% heavy element mass fractions observed in warm Jupiters.

2. Identifies outer protoplanetary disk radius as the key governing parameter: larger disk spatial extents sustain long-duration pebble fluxes that prolong inner disk vapor enrichment and maximize giant planet heavy element budgets.
3. Demonstrates that stellar host mass plays a secondary role compared to protoplanetary disk physical extent and viscosity in controlling the final heavy element mass of giant exoplanets.

4. Quantifies the impact of disk viscosity (alpha parameter) on gap-opening timescales, migration speeds, and final planet masses, illustrating how high-viscosity environments accelerate early heavy element accretion but trigger run-away gas accretion leading to brown dwarf regimes.

methodology.architecture: The study employs the custom chemcomp multi-zone chemical evolution and planet formation code (Schneider & Bitsch 2021). The model tracks one-dimensional radial disk structure over time, incorporating viscous gas evolution, dust growth, radial pebble drift, and thermal evaporation at specific temperature thresholds (ice lines for H2O, CO2, CH4, and CO). A protoplanet embedded in the disk grows via a combination of solid pebble accretion and gas accretion while undergoing type-I (un-gapped) and type-II (gap-opened) orbital migration. As drifting pebbles cross evaporation fronts, their volatile chemical constituents transition into the gas phase, raising the localized gas metallicity Z_vapor. The growing planet accretes both solid pebbles and metal-enriched gas from its feeding zone.
keyTechniques: Technique 1: Sequential Evaporation Sequence Modeling - Models the localized enrichment of gas as inward-drifting pebbles cross chemical ice lines (H2O, CO2, CH4, CO), continuously modifying the local radial metallicity Z_vapor(r, t) of the disk.

Technique 2: Hydrodynamic Planet-Disk Coupling - Integrates type-I and type-II migration rates with gap-opening criteria based on planet mass, local disk scale height, and viscous alpha parameter, accurately timing when gas accretion transitions from runaway envelope contraction to disk-accretion-limited regimes.

Technique 3: Dual Solid and Vapor Accretion Framework - Simultaneously computes solid pebble accretion onto the planetary core and enriched gas/vapor accretion into the planet envelope, tracking total heavy element mass M_heavy = M_core + M_heavy,env over time.
benchmarksUsed: Synthetic Protoplanetary Disks around Stars of 0.5 to 1.5 Solar Masses - Simulating radial disk extents from R_outer = 50 AU to 110 AU with gas masses up to 0.1 M_sun.

Interior Structure Observational Upper Bounds - Calibrated against empirical heavy element mass estimations of warm Jupiters from Thorngren et al. (2016), Müller & Helled (2025), and Peerani et al. (2026a).
methodology.mathematicalFormulation:
The total accretion rate of heavy elements onto a growing giant planet is formulated as:

M_dot_heavy(t) = M_dot_pebble(t) + Z_vapor(r_p, t) * M_dot_gas(t)

where M_dot_heavy(t) is the total mass accretion rate of heavy elements (elements heavier than H and He), M_dot_pebble(t) is the solid pebble accretion rate onto the core or envelope, Z_vapor(r_p, t) is the vapor mass fraction (metallicity) of the disk gas evaluated at the planet's orbital radius r_p at time t, and M_dot_gas(t) is the total gas accretion rate onto the planet envelope. The radial pebble mass flux driving inner disk vapor enrichment is given by:

F_pebble(r, t) = 2 * pi * r * sigma_pebble(r, t) * v_drift(r, t)

where F_pebble(r, t) is the inward mass flux of solid pebbles, sigma_pebble(r, t) is the pebble surface density, and v_drift(r, t) is the inward radial drift velocity caused by gas drag force.

quantitativeResults: Giant planets forming in large disks (R_outer = 110 AU) retain high heavy element mass accretion for over 1 Myr, accumulating up to 50-60 Earth masses of heavy elements (30-40% total planetary mass) for Jupiter-mass planets.

Disks with smaller outer radii (R_outer = 50 AU) exhaust their solid pebble reservoir significantly faster, causing inner disk vapor enrichment to decay prematurely and limiting planetary heavy element budgets to below 20-30 Earth masses.

Higher disk viscosity (alpha = 3 x 10^-4 vs 10^-4) delays gap opening, extending fast type-I migration and causing planets starting at 2 AU to cross the water ice line earlier, initial heavy element accretion rates increase for sub-Jupiter planets but deplete gas reserves faster, causing higher final gas masses (>10 Jupiter masses) approaching the brown dwarf regime.
qualitativeInsights: Pebble drift and evaporation provide a self-consistent physical mechanism that eliminates the need to invoke extreme planetesimal bombardment to explain metal-rich warm Jupiters.

Outer disk extent serves as a reservoir timer: large disk boundaries maintain a long-duration supply chain of drifting pebbles that continually replenishes inner disk vapor, decoupling planet metallicity from initial stellar host metallicity.
Stellar host mass variations (0.5 to 1.5 M_sun) have minimal direct influence on the maximum heavy element content achieved by giant planets compared to disk physical scale and viscous dynamics.

limitations: Planetesimal formation and late planetesimal accretion were excluded from the primary models to compute theoretical maximum upper bounds; planetesimal trap formation could reduce available pebble flux.

The simulations focus on single-planet systems; multi-planet systems could introduce gap competition where outer planets trap drifting pebbles, although inner planets forming sequentially maintain high metal content.

Simplified one-dimensional disk thermodynamics and parameterized boundary conditions for giant planet gap opening and gas accretion rates could introduce minor discrepancies compared to full 3D radiation-hydrodynamic simulations.
practicalImplications: Exoplanet characterization missions (JWST, Ariel) can combine atmospheric metallicity measurements with interior bulk density models to constrain the historical spatial scale and pebble drift efficiency of protoplanetary disks.

Theoretical planetary evolution codes should incorporate time-variable vapor metallicity Z_vapor(r,t) rather than assuming static solar composition gas accretion when modeling giant planet envelope formation.

keyEquationsOrTheorems.label: Heavy Element Mass Accretion Equation
keyEquationsOrTheorems.formulaOrDescription: M_dot_heavy = M_dot_pebble + Z_vapor * M_dot_gas, where M_dot_heavy is heavy element mass accretion rate, M_dot_pebble is solid pebble accretion rate, Z_vapor is local disk gas vapor fraction, and M_dot_gas is planet gas accretion rate.

keyEquationsOrTheorems.label: Radial Pebble Flux Equation
keyEquationsOrTheorems.formulaOrDescription: F_pebble = 2 * pi * r * sigma_pebble * v_drift, where F_pebble is inward pebble mass flux, r is disk radius, sigma_pebble is surface density of pebbles, and v_drift is drag-induced drift velocity.

strengths: Provides a clean, physically grounded explanation for the high heavy element fractions observed in warm Jupiters without relying on fine-tuned planetesimal collision histories.
Consistently integrates full chemical ice-line sequences, detailed planetary migration regimes, and time-dependent disk evolution using the validated chemcomp framework.
weaknesses: Does not explicitly model 3D atmospheric mixing or core-envelope dredging effects that could alter theoretical interior structure interpretations.
Assumes isolated single-planet systems in the main runs, which oversimplifies architectures where outer companion planets form early and block inner pebble drift.
potentialBiases: Focuses on maximizing the total heavy element content budget, which naturally selects parameter spaces (large disk size, uninterrupted pebble drift) optimized to hit upper observational envelope limits.

title: "Mega-Earths" are likely an artifact of stellar activity
abstract:
Draft version October 12, 2026
Typeset using LATEX twocolumn style in AASTeX631
"Mega-Earths" are likely an artifact of stellar activity
Casey L. Brinkman 1, ∗ and Nicolas B. Cowan 1
1McGill University, Trottier Space Institute, 3550 rue University, Montreal, QC, H3A 2A7, CAN
ABSTRACT
Empirical relations and planet formation simulations suggest an upper mass limit for rocky planets
of ∼10M⊕, as cores above this will almost certainly undergo runaway gas accretion. Nevertheless, a
small number of planets appear to have densities consistent with rocky Earth-like compositions above
this threshold, indicating that unusual formation and evolutionary scenarios are capable of producing
extremely massive rocky planets called "Mega-Earths." However, all of these planets orbit active stars
with logR′
HK >-4.75. We find a <1% probability that all literature ultra-massive rocky planets would
coincidentally orbit such active stars, and find no astrophysical reason to expect Mega-Earths to
preferentially form around active stars. We therefore conclude that Mega-Earths are artifacts of stellar
activity, and we question the reliability of Gaussian Processes to enable mass measurements for rocky
planets around active stars.

sections.name: Introduction
sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The diversity of rocky planet masses, radii, and den-
sities inform our understanding of planet formation and
evolution pathways. Rocky planets can either be formed
primordially (Lee et al. 2014; Cloutier & Menou 2020),
or as the stripped cores of larger sub-Neptunes whose en-
velopes were likely lost through core-powered mass loss
(Ginzburg et al. 2018), photoevaporation from their host
star (Owen & Wu 2017), or a combination of phenomena
(Rogers et al. 2021). The transition from rocky to gas-
rich planets is a natural product of core-accretion the-
ory: once a growing planetary core exceeds several Earth
masses, it can no longer avoid runaway gas accretion
from the surrounding protoplanetary disk, whereby mas-
sive planets necessarily form gaseous envelopes (Mizuno
1980).
Empirically, the mass and radius measurements of
small planets suggest a transition between planets con-
sistent with a bare rocky composition devoid of sig-
nificant volatile content, and those likely hosting en-
velopes at R = 1.5 − 1.75R⊕ (Weiss & Marcy 2014;
Lopez & Fortney 2014; Rogers 2015; Fulton et al. 2017).
This transition point in planet mass occurs between
M = 4 − 5M⊕, and appears to be the minimum mass
Corresponding author: Casey L. Brinkman
casey.brinkman@mcgill.ca
∗ TSI Postdoctoral Fellow
needed to accrete substantial quantities of volatile ele-
ments (Otegi et al. 2020; Müller et al. 2024).
This empirical transition happens at masses far lower
than the theoretical limit derived from planet forma-
tion theories. Simulations of collisional mantle stripping
and post-formation erosion suggest that even under ex-
treme conditions, the maximum mass for a primordial
rocky planet is unlikely to exceed ∼10 M⊕ (Pollack et al.
1996; Lee & Owen 2025; Reinhardt et al. 2022). This
cutoff boundary is a function of disk composition, stellar
flux, etc. The existence of an ultra-massive rocky planet
beyond this threshold would require either exceptional
formation environments or extreme evolutionary path-
ways, and would imply interior conditions potentially
unlike other rocky worlds.
In recent years, several exoplanet characterization ef-
forts have yielded mass and radius measurements consis-
tent with volatile-poor densities, but with masses larger
than 10 M⊕, occasionally referred to as "Mega-Earths."
These planets could potentially form collisionally post
disk-dispersal thereby escaping runaway gas accretion
(Lee & Chiang 2015), or they could be remnant photo-
evaporated cores of former giants (Armstrong et al.
2020). Our certainty that these strange objects even
exist, however, is only as strong as the quality of the
mass and radius measurements and therefore our ability
to characterize the host star.
Magnetically active stars notoriously complicate stel-
lar characterization and challenge RV mass determina-
tion. Active regions can suppress convection in the star,

ble of masking the smaller semi-amplitudes produced by
small, rocky planets. Star spots (and plages) can mimic
the signature of an orbiting planet as the star rotates,
and this added jitter can artificially inflate the RV sig-
nal of a transiting planet or bury it beneath noise, often
leading to erroneously large planet masses (Dumusque
et al. 2011a,b).
In this work, we use literature masses and radii of
small planets to identify potential "Mega-Earth" plan-
ets beyond the runaway gas accretion threshold. We
then analyze the likelihood of their existence given the
context of their host star activity.
2. MEGA-EARTHS AND THE SMALL PLANET
POPULATION
2.1. Sample Curation
To identify planets in the rocky planet density regime,
we selected planets between 0–4 R⊕ that have published
masses and radii using the NASA Exoplanet Archive
(Akeson et al. 2013, queried 7/15/2025). First, we re-
moved any planets with only mass upper limits, nontran-
siting msin(i) values, or masses produced using mass-
radius relationships. Next, we removed planets with
fractional uncertainties on mass larger than 50%. Lastly,
we removed planets with masses measured using transit
timing tariations (TTVs), as TTVs—particularly from
large surveys—often predict unphysically high planet
masses that are unable to be validated through other
methods, and are more reliable for mass ratios between
planets than absolute masses (Mills & Mazeh 2017; Jin
et al. 2026). The radii and radial velocity (RV) masses of
our resulting sample of 333 planets are shown in Figure
1.
2.2. Anomalously Massive Rocky Planets
As expected, the vast majority of well-characterized
rocky planet masses fall below 10 M⊕, and the majority
of planets more massive than this threshold are consis-
tent with gas-rich compositions. We identify 4 planets
with mass measurements exceeding 10 M⊕ and a radius
consistent with a volatile-poor rocky composition, here-
after referred to as Mega-Earths: WASP-84 c, TOI-1347
b, TOI-2322 c, and HD 63433 b.
We also consider GJ 523 b, despite sitting just out-
side the rocky planet density regime and therefore con-
sistent with a modest gaseous envelope, as Kroft et al.
-- 2 of 12 --

Figure 2. TESS lightcurves (PDCSAP Flux) of each Mega-Earth host star are shown, demonstrating visible rotational modu-
lation due to stellar activity.
(2026) identify this ultra-dense Neptune-sized object as
a "Mega-Earth." Interior modeling suggests a Hycean
(21% water mass) composition with little to no H/He
envelope, assuming a standard four-layer planet com-
position (core, mantle, water layer, and H/He envelope)
and an Earth-like ratio of iron to refractory abundances.
Sitting near GJ 523 b in mass-radius space are three ad-
ditional worlds worth considering: TOI-815 c, HD 18599
b, and GJ 143 b. Given that these worlds likely host
little H/He envelope despite having sufficient mass to
trigger runaway gas accretion we include them in this
analysis. 1 The eight planets identified as anomylously
dense are highlighted in Figurer 1.
We quantify the distribution of planet masses and
radii in our sample using a two-dimensional Gaus-
sian Kernel Density Estimate (hereafter KDE) using
SciPy.stats. To calculate the highest probability radii
for any given value of planet mass p(R|M), we gener-
ated grids of planet radii from 0.001 to 4 R⊕ and planet
1 HD 119130 b was originally found to have similar masses and
radii, but Akana Murphy et al. (2025) recently found this mass
artificially inflated by a factor of three due to constructive inter-
ference with an untreated sinusoidal signal in the data such as

mass from 0.001 to 50 M⊕ and then evaluated the KDE
at each mass over the full grid of planetary radii. We
then normalized this distribution over radius to get the
conditional probability of radius for each slice in mass.
The resulting probability density and our eight Mega-
Earths are shown in Figure 1.
All eight Mega-Earths considered here correspond to
probabilities <0.1, indicating that they have some of
the most anomalous combinations of mass and radius
of those in our sample. The planet corresponding to
the lowest probability density is HD 63433 b (0.006),
followed by HD 18599 b (0.007).
2.3. WASP-84 c
WASP-84 is 1–2 Gyr old K0 star hosting a transiting
warm Jupiter and a recently discovered interior planet
at an orbital period of P = 1.44 days with a radius of
Rc = 1.95 ± 0.12R⊕ and a mass of Mc = 15.2 ± 4.5M⊕
(Maciejewski et al. 2023). The mass and radius mea-
surements suggest an interior composition more iron-
rich than the Earth, and the authors have dubbed this
object a hot super-Earth. Complicating the RV analysis,
WASP-84 exhibits chromospheric activity (logR′
HK =
−4.42 ± 0.04) and starspots produce noticeable rota-
tional modulation (Prot = 14.36 days) in the TESS
lightcurve (Fig 2). Correspondingly, the authors re-
port significant RV jitter of ∼13 m/s for the RV dataset,
larger than the planetary signal (Kb = 7.7 m/s).
WASP-84 hosts not only a supposed Mega-Earth but
also a warm Jupiter—neither of which likely formed in-
situ. Interestingly, both planets have negligible eccen-
tricity. Due to their well aligned orbits, both planets are
thought to have migrated inwards through interactions
with the proto-planetary disk, reducing the likelihood
for chaotic post-disk-dispersal collisions (Anderson et al.
2015).
2.4. TOI-1347 b
TOI-1347 is a 1-2 Gyr old, moderately active
(logR′
HK = −4.66) G-type star hosting an ultra-short
period planet with a radius of Rc = 1.8 ± 0.1R⊕ and
a mass of Mc = 11.1 ± 1.2M⊕ (Rubenzahl et al. 2024).
Lomb-scargle periodograms of both the photometry and
RVs exhibit significant power at ∼8 days and at the
likely stellar rotation period Prot = 16.34 ± 0.57 days.
The orbital period of planet b, Porb = 0.85 days, is
thankfully much shorter than the rotational period of
the star. The RV semi-amplitude (Kb = 7.74 m/s) mea-
sured using 134 RVs from the HIRES and HARPS-N
spectrographs, however, is of similar order to the RV
jitter (σ= 4.05 and 8.2 m/s respectively for HIRES and
HARPS-N).
The mass and radius measurements for TOI-1347 b
suggest a bulk composition similar to that of Earth, and
due to the mass and equilibrium temperature (Teq =
1400 ± 40 K), a H/He envelope can be ruled out with
confidence. However, the phase curve in TESS photome-
try exhibits a secondary eclipse depth suggestive of heat
transport through a gaseous envelope (Rubenzahl et al.
2024), despite being sufficiently old for any primordial
H/He envelope to have evaporated. This suggests the
presence of a higher mean molecular weight envelope,
necessitating the inner core to be even more dense than
suggested by mass-radius curves.
2.5. TOI-2322 c
TOI-2322 is a moderately active K-dwarf (logR’HK =
−4.59) hosting two transiting rocky planets. While
the inner rocky planet has a virtually unconstrained
mass (Mb = 2.31 ± 2.6M⊕), the outer has a radius of
Rc = 1.87 ± 0.66R⊕ and a mass of Mc = 18.1 ± 4.34M⊕
(Hobson et al. 2025). The RV semi-amplitude of planet
c (Kc = 5.37±1.6 m/s), measured using 52 RVs from the
ESPRESSO and HARPS-N spectrographs, is of similar
scale to the RV jitter (σ = 7.4 and 4.07 m/s, respectively
for ESPRESSO and HARPS-N).
The rotational period of the star (Prot = 21.28 ± 0.08
days) is visible in the TESS light curves (Figure 2),
and disconcertingly coincides with the orbital period of
TOI-2322 c (Porbc = 20.23 days). The orbital period of
the inner planet, TOI-2322 b, is roughly half this value
(Porbb = 11.31 days). To attempt to disentangle these
signals, Hobson et al. (2025) use a multivariate GP to
simultaneously fit the photometry and RVs, as well as
full-width half max and the bisector inverse slope activ-
ity indicators.
2.6. HD 63433 b
HD 63433 is a young (∼400 Myr) G-type star hosting
three transiting planets (Mann et al. 2020; Capistrant
et al. 2024). HD 63433 b has the largest RV mass of
any discussed here at Mb = 37.3 ± 9.6M⊕ with a radius
of Rb = 2.16 ± 0.05R⊕ (Polanski et al. 2024a). This
measurement was obtained by fitting 62 RVs from the
HIRES and APF spectrographs, although notably Mal-
lorquín et al. (2023) do not measure a semi-amplitude
for this planet using CARMENES RVs and report 3σ
upper limit of Mb < 21M⊕. Both RV analyses use GPs
informed by photometry.
The planet semi-amplitude measured is Kb = 12.5 ±
3.2, which is similar in amplitude to the stellar jitter
from HIRES (σ = 15 m/s) and APF (σ = 5.0). The ro-
tational period of the host star (Prot = 6.45 days) is close
to the orbital period of HD 63433 b (Porb = 7.1 days),

2.7. GJ 523 b
With a mass of Mb = 23.5 ± 3.3M⊕ and a radius of

young (169 Myr), magnetically active star, though nei-

GJ 523 b has an inclined orbit with respect to its
