2.8. TOI-815 c
The discovery paper for TOI-815 c reports a Rc =
2.94 ± 0.15R⊕ planet with a mass of Mc = 23.5 ±
2.5M⊕, along with a much less dense companion
(Mb = 7.6 ± 1.5M⊕, similar radius) using 34 RVs
from VLT/ESPRESSO (Psaridi et al. 2024). The semi-
amplitude of planet c (Kc = 5.5 ± 0.5 m/s) is nearly
three times the reported RV jitter (1.88 m/s). These
planets orbit a young (0.2 Gyr) magnetically active K-
dwarf with a reported median logR′
HK = −4.67 ± 0.03.
The rotation period of the star (Prot = 15.2±1.2 days) is
nearly half the orbital period of TOI-815 c (Porb = 34.9
days), while the inner, lower density sub-Neptune has
an orbital period of 11 days. To address the effects of

2.9. HD 18599 b
HD 18599 b is Rb = 2.60 ± 0.15R⊕ planet with a re-

period of HD 18599 (Prot = 8.73 ± 0.7 days) is roughly
double the orbital period of planet b (Porb = 4.14 days),
and the authors use a quasi-perioid GP kernel to account
for the effects of this activity on the RV signal. Desidera
et al. (2023) compare the high density of this planet to
that of Kepler-411 b (with a TTV derived mass, (Sun

2.10. GJ 143 b
GJ 143 b has a radius of Rb = 2.61 ± 0.17R⊕ and
a mass of Mb = 22.7 ± 2.2M⊕ (Dragomir et al. 2019)
measured using a total of 140 RVs from HARPS and
PFS. It orbits an active K-dwarf (logR′
HK = −4.42 ±
0.05, Boro Saikia et al. (2018)), with an orbital period
nearly identical to the rotational period of its host star
(35 days). The measured semi-amplitude (Kb = 5.51 ±
0.41 m/s) is larger than the reported RV jitter (1.44
m/s). The authors use a Gaussian Process (celerite
kernel) fitting the RVs and photometry simultaneously
to account for the effects of stellar activity.
3. STELLAR ACTIVITY AND PLANET MASS
3.1. Mass vs logR′
HK
All five of these Mega-Earths were identified as orbit-
ing active stars in their respective discovery papers. We
downloaded the TESS light curves for each target using
the Lightkurve Python package (Lightkurve Collabora-
tion et al. 2018). We removed NaN values, normalized
the flux, binned the light curves by 35 cadences, and
flattened the resulting light curves using a 1001-point
window to remove long-term instrumental and system-
atic trends. We then removed > 6σ outliers and used the
resulting light curves to visualize the rotational modu-
lation of each host star (Figure 2).
In order to compare with the general population of
normal-mass rocky planets, we identify literature values
of logR′
HK for 33 of the planets consistent with a rocky
planet density in our dataset (Table 1), including four
of the five identified Mega-Earths. We use logR′
HK as
a tracer for magnetic activity in the host star, as the
Ca II H & K lines are particularly sensitive to magnetic
heating in the chromosphere, producing greater flux in
the cores of these lines.
For GJ 523, no value for logR′
HK has been published—
however, we can estimate the value using a typical
Rossby number for a young (∼160 Myr), rapidly ro-
tating (Prot = 5.621 d) K-dwarf and the relationship
established in Mamajek & Hillenbrand (2008). The
Rossby number is defined as R0 = Prot
τc , where τc is the
convective turnover time. We estimate this timescale
using B-V color magnitudes and Equation 4 in Noyes
et al. (1984). We find a B-V of ∼1.0 (Stassun et al.
2019), which suggests a convective timescale of τc = 23
days. This would then correspond to a Rossby number
of ∼0.25, and according to Fig. 7 and Equation 6 of Ma-
majek & Hillenbrand (2008) GJ 523 likely has a value of
logR′
HK = −4.33. We adopt a conservative uncertainty
estimate of 0.1 to account for systematics.
We plot the literature values of planet mass as a
function of logR′
HK in Figure 3. We use the regions
of logR′
HK that were identified in Henry et al. (1996)
to determine if host stars are inactive, quiet, active,
or very active, with logR′
HK =-4.75 corresponding to
the boundary between quiet and active stars (Vaughn-
Preston Gap) (Pace et al. 2009). While 24 stars fall in
the inactive and quiet regions and 13 fall in the active re-
gion, all eight rocky and volatile-rich Mega-Earths orbit
active stars with logR′
HK > −4.75.
If the underlying distribution of Mega-Earths across
stellar activity levels was uniform, we would expect an
equal likelihood of finding a mega-Earth around any star
in our sample, regardless of activity. Considering first
just the four rocky-density Mega-Earths, we can calcu-
late the likelihood that they happen to orbit stars with
logR′
HK > −4.75. The odds that a single Mega-Earth
orbits an active star in our sample is 13/37, as we have
mass and logR′
HK values for 37 stars, 13 of which fall
above the Vaughan-Preston gap. The odds that all four
orbit active stars are:

3.2. Should young stars preferentially host
mega-Earths?
Stellar chromospheric activity from calcium H and K
lines is inversely associated with age (Wilson 1963; Ma-
majek & Hillenbrand 2008). We expect certain cate-
gories of planets, such as inflated gas giants (Benatti
et al. 2019) or those with primordial H/He envelopes
(Rogers 2025) to be more commonly observed around
young stars. What about Mega-Earths?
The hypothesized pathways to produce dense rocky
bodies more massive than 10 M⊕ require timescales con-
sistent with, if not beyond that of traditional super-
Earths. One method of circumventing runaway gas ac-
cretion is to form in a gas-free environment. For sun-like
stars in clusters, roughly 80% are disk bearing at 1 Myr,
50-60% at 2-3 Myr, and only 5% at 10 Myr, with a typi-
cal disk lifetime of 5.8 ± 0.3 Myr (Polnitzky et al. 2026;
Rab et al. 2016). While drag from the planet-forming
disk helps to keep orbits circularized, many planets ex-
perience spikes in eccentricity as the disk disperses, trig-
gering a period of giant impacts that turn planetesimals
into planets. This period lasted ∼100 Myrs in the case
of the solar system (Genda et al. 2015; Kimura et al.
2025). All rocky planets form from planetesimals dur-
ing this phase–but to build a volatile-free planet with
M>10 ⊕, a larger than average number of planetesimal
collisions are likely needed, requiring additional forma-
tion time, on average.
More problematic than the assembly timescale is the
likelihood that these planets had to migrate inwards to
their present day orbits. The Mega-Earths discussed
here have orbits of 0.8–20 days, and the available solid
inventory is almost certainly insufficient to form such
massive planetary cores in situ (Izidoro et al. 2014).
Smooth, low-eccentricity migration typically happens
within the planet forming disk for massive planets that
accreted rapidly (Kley et al. 2012), while higher eccen-
tricity migration typically occurs post disk dispersal and
requires subsequent tidal dissipation to produce circu-
lar orbits (Dawson & Johnson 2018), at least for giant
planets. For rocky planets, planetary embryos likely mi-
grated through the disk only to form planets post disk
dispersal (Cossou et al. 2014). The Mega-Earths in our
sample all have nearly circular orbits, despite circular-
ization timescales comparable to the stellar ages from a
few Myr to several Gyr (Dawson & Johnson 2018).
The second pathway to build a Mega-Earth is to form
a giant planet with a gas-rich envelope and subsequently
strip away the gas (Armstrong et al. 2020; Biersteker &
Schlichting 2019)—a process which would also require
the migration of a planet inwards. This stripping would
almost certainly have to occur post disk-dispersal, given
the high energy collisions needed to strip a giant planet’s
envelope and to avoid the resulting core re-accreting an
envelope. Therefore high eccentricity migration would
likely be necessary, requiring longer re-circularization
times.
The formation timescales of Mega-Earths are therefore
at least as long as super-Earths, and there is no reason
to believe that they would be likely to be destroyed or
undergo a change in mass or radius through the lifetime
of the planet. We therefore would not expect young
stars to preferentially host these worlds, and predict at
minimum a uniform distribution of Mega-Earths across
host star age and activity level if not a preference toward
older systems.
3.3. Are Mega-Earths a product of stellar activity?
The remaining and most probable explanation for
the fact that we observe several rocky planets with
M>10M⊕ around active stars is that stellar activity has
artificially inflated the RV mass measurements. Stel-
lar activity introduces additional scatter to RV datasets,
producing a fundamental noise floor (Isaacson & Fischer
2010)–therefore we are less sensitive to planetary signals
around an active star than we are to the planets with the
same semi-amplitude around a magnetically quiet star
of similar spectral type, size, and distance from Earth.
When we couple this with our bias toward detecting and
measuring larger semi-amplitudes over small ones that
get swallowed up in the noise (Dumusque et al. 2011b,a),
as well as our bias toward publishing statistically sig-
nificant planet detections with larger k/σk ratios, this

The predominant method used to fit the stellar
variability—thereby allowing a more faithful interpre-
tation of the planetary RV signals—is Gaussian Process
(GP) Regression (Dumusque et al. 2011b). GP regres-
sion describes the correlation between data through a
covariance matrix and was introduced to the field of ex-
oplanets in 2011 to model correlated noise from instru-
ment systematics (Gibson et al. 2012), and subsequently
used to model correlated stellar variability due to the ro-
tation and evolution of star spots (Haywood et al. 2014).
This method has been widely employed to produce mass
measurements of small planets around active stars, in-
cluding Kepler-78 b (Grunblatt et al. 2016) and K2-291
b (Kosiarek et al. 2019), amongst many more.

However, our ability to disentangle these signals
depends on the relative strengths of the RV semi-
amplitude and stellar activity amplitude, the difference
in the planet’s orbital period and stellar rotation pe-
riod, our ability to constrain these parameters and place
meaningful priors on our GP, and the thoroughness
of RV sampling and observing cadence. Overly flex-
ible GPs can overfit an RV dataset, absorbing signal
as stellar noise, often producing larger than expected
planet semi-amplitudes and therefore masses (Blunt
et al. 2023).
The original analyses of all eight Mega-Earths above
utilize GPs with various kernel forms (Celerite, Quasi-
Periodic, 3/2 Matern, etc.), and all utilize prior con-
straints on rotational period and spot decay timescales
informed by photometry. Despite taking all usual mea-
sures to ensure that the effects of stellar activity are
accounted for in their RV analysis, the remaining mass
measurements for these five planets remain improbably
large. This calls into question our ability to fully ac-
count for the effects of stellar activity even when using
well-constrained GPs.
Dumusque et al. (2017) identify a critical threshold of
signal to noise where GPs can reliably recover the under-
lying planetary RV signal from a noisy dataset. They
find a critical threshold at K/N = Kpl
RVrms
√Nobs = 5,
but recommend a threshold of 7.5 for reliably detecting
signals. Of the five Mega-Earths identified here, three
fall below this threshold (WASP-84 c: 3.8, TOI-2322 c:
6.5, HD 63433 b: 5.3). HD 18599 b falls exactly at the
7.5 threshold, while the rest fall above with a range of
11-16.
The systems where the orbital period of the planet—
or harmonics thereof—is similar to the rotational period
of the star are the most challenging to characterize, as
any signal at these periods will be most enhanced by
stellar activity. Of our Mega-Earth sample, GJ 143 b,
HD 63433 b, and TOI-2322 c have an orbital period
similar to the rotational period of their host star, while
HD 18599 b and TOI-815 c orbit at harmonics of this
value. Polanski et al. (2024b) acknowledge this challenge
with HD 63433 b and caution putting faith in a RV-
derived mass even with a well-informed GP.
Despite having easily separable stellar rotation peri-
ods and planetary orbital periods, the remaining three
planets are likely to have RV signals inflated by stellar
activity. Looking forward, there is promise to better ac-
count for stellar activity using GPs when RVs are strate-
gically scheduled to optimize the sampling of both mag-
netic activity and exoplanetary signals, that way both
are more easily modeled (López-Morales et al. 2016; Bar-
ros et al. 2017; Nava et al. 2020). In particular, schedul-
ing high-cadence RV measurements for short and ultra-
short period planets with a nightly RV baseline offset
could allow for a reduction in the effects of stellar activ-
ity on RV mass determination.
4. CONCLUSIONS
We analyze the population of planets with radii<4
R⊕ and find four worlds consistent with a rocky planet
density that appear to be more massive than the gas-
accretion threshold (∼10 M⊕). We find four addi-
tional planets over this threshold that likely host dense
volatile-rich atmospheres inconsistent with significant
H/He content. These planets would require unusual for-
mation pathways, such as orbital migration and enve-
lope stripping or a series of larger than expected colli-
sions post disk-dispersal. However, we find:
• All eight Mega-Earths with M> 10M⊕ orbit active
stars with logR′
HK > −4.75.
• There is no physical reason for Mega-Earths to
prefer younger more active host stars—if anything,
these worlds should prefer older systems to allow
time for these unusal evolutionary pathways.
• We calculate a < 1% likelihood that these mega-
Earths coincidentally orbit exclusively active stars.
• The most likely culprit for these larger than ex-
pected masses is artificial inflation from stellar
activity—particularly for systems that have sim-
ilar stellar rotation and planetary orbital periods.
• Therefore, there is no compelling evidence for
rocky planets forming above the upper mass limit
of 10M⊕.
The mass measurements for these five worlds utilize
photometrically informed Gaussian Processes to help
disentangle stellar noise from planetary signal. Ul-
timately, despite our best efforts to characterize and
fit stellar activity, we should remain skeptical of RV
mass measurements for planets orbiting active stars—
particularly so when the existence of such planets would
challenge our notions of planet formation.
5. ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
We would like to thank Andrew Cumming, Sabina
Sagynbayeva, and Charles-Edouard Boukaré for helpful
conversations.

chunks.heading: Abstract
chunks.text:
Draft version October 12, 2026
Typeset using LATEX twocolumn style in AASTeX631
"Mega-Earths" are likely an artifact of stellar activity
Casey L. Brinkman 1, ∗ and Nicolas B. Cowan 1
1McGill University, Trottier Space Institute, 3550 rue University, Montreal, QC, H3A 2A7, CAN
ABSTRACT
Empirical relations and planet formation simulations suggest an upper mass limit for rocky planets
of ∼10M⊕, as cores above this will almost certainly undergo runaway gas accretion. Nevertheless, a
small number of planets appear to have densities consistent with rocky Earth-like compositions above
this threshold, indicating that unusual formation and evolutionary scenarios are capable of producing
extremely massive rocky planets called "Mega-Earths." However, all of these planets orbit active stars
with logR′
HK >-4.75. We find a <1% probability that all literature ultra-massive rocky planets would
coincidentally orbit such active stars, and find no astrophysical reason to expect Mega-Earths to
preferentially form around active stars. We therefore conclude that Mega-Earths are artifacts of stellar
activity, and we question the reliability of Gaussian Processes to enable mass measurements for rocky
planets around active stars.

chunks.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
chunks.text:
The diversity of rocky planet masses, radii, and den-
sities inform our understanding of planet formation and
evolution pathways. Rocky planets can either be formed
primordially (Lee et al. 2014; Cloutier & Menou 2020),
or as the stripped cores of larger sub-Neptunes whose en-
velopes were likely lost through core-powered mass loss
(Ginzburg et al. 2018), photoevaporation from their host
star (Owen & Wu 2017), or a combination of phenomena
(Rogers et al. 2021). The transition from rocky to gas-
rich planets is a natural product of core-accretion the-
ory: once a growing planetary core exceeds several Earth
masses, it can no longer avoid runaway gas accretion
from the surrounding protoplanetary disk, whereby mas-
sive planets necessarily form gaseous envelopes (Mizuno
1980).
Empirically, the mass and radius measurements of
small planets suggest a transition between planets con-
sistent with a bare rocky composition devoid of sig-
nificant volatile content, and those likely hosting en-
velopes at R = 1.5 − 1.75R⊕ (Weiss & Marcy 2014;
Lopez & Fortney 2014; Rogers 2015; Fulton et al. 2017).
This transition point in planet mass occurs between
M = 4 − 5M⊕, and appears to be the minimum mass
Corresponding author: Casey L. Brinkman
casey.brinkman@mcgill.ca
∗ TSI Postdoctoral Fellow
needed to accrete substantial quantities of volatile ele-
ments (Otegi et al. 2020; Müller et al. 2024).
This empirical transition happens at masses far lower
than the theoretical limit derived from planet forma-
tion theories. Simulations of collisional mantle stripping
and post-formation erosion suggest that even under ex-
treme conditions, the maximum mass for a primordial
rocky planet is unlikely to exceed ∼10 M⊕ (Pollack et al.
1996; Lee & Owen 2025; Reinhardt et al. 2022). This
cutoff boundary is a function of disk composition, stellar
flux, etc. The existence of an ultra-massive rocky planet
beyond this threshold would require either exceptional
formation environments or extreme evolutionary path-
ways, and would imply interior conditions potentially
unlike other rocky worlds.
In recent years, several exoplanet characterization ef-
forts have yielded mass and radius measurements consis-
tent with volatile-poor densities, but with masses larger
than 10 M⊕, occasionally referred to as "Mega-Earths."
These planets could potentially form collisionally post
disk-dispersal thereby escaping runaway gas accretion
(Lee & Chiang 2015), or they could be remnant photo-
evaporated cores of former giants (Armstrong et al.
2020). Our certainty that these strange objects even
exist, however, is only as strong as the quality of the
mass and radius measurements and therefore our ability
to characterize the host star.
Magnetically active stars notoriously complicate stel-
lar characterization and challenge RV mass determina-
tion. Active regions can suppress convection in the star,

2 Brinkman et al.
Figure 1. Planet radius vs. mass for small planets (< 4R⊕) are plotted as grey points. Lines show mass-radius relations for
planets with an Earth-like composition, a purely silicate-rock composition, and a purely iron composition (Zeng et al. 2019),
representing the possible mass-radius space in which rocky planets can exist. Literature values come from the NASA Exoplanet
Archive (Akeson et al. 2013) queried 7/15/2026 for planets with mass and radius measurements with fractional uncertainties
<30%. The colormap represents the normalized probability density estimated from a Gaussian KDE. We show the theoretical
maximum rocky planet mass threshold (10 M⊕) and identify planets above this threshold in the rocky planet density regime as
possible Mega-Earths(white circles).
producing erroneous RV measurements and are capa-
ble of masking the smaller semi-amplitudes produced by
small, rocky planets. Star spots (and plages) can mimic
the signature of an orbiting planet as the star rotates,
and this added jitter can artificially inflate the RV sig-
nal of a transiting planet or bury it beneath noise, often
leading to erroneously large planet masses (Dumusque
et al. 2011a,b).
In this work, we use literature masses and radii of
small planets to identify potential "Mega-Earth" plan-
ets beyond the runaway gas accretion threshold. We
then analyze the likelihood of their existence given the
context of their host star activity.
2. MEGA-EARTHS AND THE SMALL PLANET
POPULATION
2.1. Sample Curation
To identify planets in the rocky planet density regime,
we selected planets between 0–4 R⊕ that have published
masses and radii using the NASA Exoplanet Archive
(Akeson et al. 2013, queried 7/15/2025). First, we re-
moved any planets with only mass upper limits, nontran-
siting msin(i) values, or masses produced using mass-
radius relationships. Next, we removed planets with
fractional uncertainties on mass larger than 50%. Lastly,
we removed planets with masses measured using transit
timing tariations (TTVs), as TTVs—particularly from
large surveys—often predict unphysically high planet
masses that are unable to be validated through other
methods, and are more reliable for mass ratios between
planets than absolute masses (Mills & Mazeh 2017; Jin
et al. 2026). The radii and radial velocity (RV) masses of
our resulting sample of 333 planets are shown in Figure
1.

2.3. WASP-84 c
WASP-84 is 1–2 Gyr old K0 star hosting a transiting
warm Jupiter and a recently discovered interior planet
at an orbital period of P = 1.44 days with a radius of
Rc = 1.95 ± 0.12R⊕ and a mass of Mc = 15.2 ± 4.5M⊕
(Maciejewski et al. 2023). The mass and radius mea-
surements suggest an interior composition more iron-
rich than the Earth, and the authors have dubbed this
object a hot super-Earth. Complicating the RV analysis,
WASP-84 exhibits chromospheric activity (logR′
HK =
−4.42 ± 0.04) and starspots produce noticeable rota-
tional modulation (Prot = 14.36 days) in the TESS
lightcurve (Fig 2). Correspondingly, the authors re-
port significant RV jitter of ∼13 m/s for the RV dataset,
larger than the planetary signal (Kb = 7.7 m/s).
WASP-84 hosts not only a supposed Mega-Earth but
also a warm Jupiter—neither of which likely formed in-
situ. Interestingly, both planets have negligible eccen-
tricity. Due to their well aligned orbits, both planets are
thought to have migrated inwards through interactions
with the proto-planetary disk, reducing the likelihood
for chaotic post-disk-dispersal collisions (Anderson et al.
2015).
2.4. TOI-1347 b
TOI-1347 is a 1-2 Gyr old, moderately active
(logR′
HK = −4.66) G-type star hosting an ultra-short
period planet with a radius of Rc = 1.8 ± 0.1R⊕ and
a mass of Mc = 11.1 ± 1.2M⊕ (Rubenzahl et al. 2024).
Lomb-scargle periodograms of both the photometry and
RVs exhibit significant power at ∼8 days and at the
likely stellar rotation period Prot = 16.34 ± 0.57 days.
The orbital period of planet b, Porb = 0.85 days, is
thankfully much shorter than the rotational period of
the star. The RV semi-amplitude (Kb = 7.74 m/s) mea-
sured using 134 RVs from the HIRES and HARPS-N
spectrographs, however, is of similar order to the RV
jitter (σ= 4.05 and 8.2 m/s respectively for HIRES and
HARPS-N).
The mass and radius measurements for TOI-1347 b
suggest a bulk composition similar to that of Earth, and
due to the mass and equilibrium temperature (Teq =
1400 ± 40 K), a H/He envelope can be ruled out with
confidence. However, the phase curve in TESS photome-
try exhibits a secondary eclipse depth suggestive of heat
transport through a gaseous envelope (Rubenzahl et al.
2024), despite being sufficiently old for any primordial
H/He envelope to have evaporated. This suggests the
presence of a higher mean molecular weight envelope,
necessitating the inner core to be even more dense than
suggested by mass-radius curves.

3. STELLAR ACTIVITY AND PLANET MASS
3.1. Mass vs logR′
HK
All five of these Mega-Earths were identified as orbit-
ing active stars in their respective discovery papers. We
downloaded the TESS light curves for each target using
the Lightkurve Python package (Lightkurve Collabora-
tion et al. 2018). We removed NaN values, normalized
the flux, binned the light curves by 35 cadences, and
flattened the resulting light curves using a 1001-point
window to remove long-term instrumental and system-
atic trends. We then removed > 6σ outliers and used the
resulting light curves to visualize the rotational modu-
lation of each host star (Figure 2).
In order to compare with the general population of
normal-mass rocky planets, we identify literature values
of logR′
HK for 33 of the planets consistent with a rocky
planet density in our dataset (Table 1), including four
of the five identified Mega-Earths. We use logR′
HK as
a tracer for magnetic activity in the host star, as the
Ca II H & K lines are particularly sensitive to magnetic
heating in the chromosphere, producing greater flux in
the cores of these lines.
For GJ 523, no value for logR′
HK has been published—
however, we can estimate the value using a typical
Rossby number for a young (∼160 Myr), rapidly ro-
tating (Prot = 5.621 d) K-dwarf and the relationship
established in Mamajek & Hillenbrand (2008). The
Rossby number is defined as R0 = Prot
τc , where τc is the
convective turnover time. We estimate this timescale
using B-V color magnitudes and Equation 4 in Noyes
et al. (1984). We find a B-V of ∼1.0 (Stassun et al.
2019), which suggests a convective timescale of τc = 23
days. This would then correspond to a Rossby number
of ∼0.25, and according to Fig. 7 and Equation 6 of Ma-
majek & Hillenbrand (2008) GJ 523 likely has a value of
logR′
HK = −4.33. We adopt a conservative uncertainty
estimate of 0.1 to account for systematics.
We plot the literature values of planet mass as a
function of logR′
HK in Figure 3. We use the regions
of logR′
HK that were identified in Henry et al. (1996)
to determine if host stars are inactive, quiet, active,
or very active, with logR′
HK =-4.75 corresponding to
the boundary between quiet and active stars (Vaughn-
Preston Gap) (Pace et al. 2009). While 24 stars fall in
the inactive and quiet regions and 13 fall in the active re-
gion, all eight rocky and volatile-rich Mega-Earths orbit
active stars with logR′
HK > −4.75.

logR′

mass and logR′

3.2. Should young stars preferentially host
mega-Earths?
Stellar chromospheric activity from calcium H and K
lines is inversely associated with age (Wilson 1963; Ma-
majek & Hillenbrand 2008). We expect certain cate-
gories of planets, such as inflated gas giants (Benatti
et al. 2019) or those with primordial H/He envelopes
(Rogers 2025) to be more commonly observed around
young stars. What about Mega-Earths?
The hypothesized pathways to produce dense rocky
bodies more massive than 10 M⊕ require timescales con-
sistent with, if not beyond that of traditional super-
Earths. One method of circumventing runaway gas ac-
cretion is to form in a gas-free environment. For sun-like
stars in clusters, roughly 80% are disk bearing at 1 Myr,
50-60% at 2-3 Myr, and only 5% at 10 Myr, with a typi-
cal disk lifetime of 5.8 ± 0.3 Myr (Polnitzky et al. 2026;
Rab et al. 2016). While drag from the planet-forming
disk helps to keep orbits circularized, many planets ex-
perience spikes in eccentricity as the disk disperses, trig-
gering a period of giant impacts that turn planetesimals
into planets. This period lasted ∼100 Myrs in the case
of the solar system (Genda et al. 2015; Kimura et al.
2025). All rocky planets form from planetesimals dur-
ing this phase–but to build a volatile-free planet with
M>10 ⊕, a larger than average number of planetesimal
collisions are likely needed, requiring additional forma-
tion time, on average.
More problematic than the assembly timescale is the
likelihood that these planets had to migrate inwards to
their present day orbits. The Mega-Earths discussed
here have orbits of 0.8–20 days, and the available solid
inventory is almost certainly insufficient to form such
massive planetary cores in situ (Izidoro et al. 2014).
Smooth, low-eccentricity migration typically happens
within the planet forming disk for massive planets that
accreted rapidly (Kley et al. 2012), while higher eccen-
tricity migration typically occurs post disk dispersal and
requires subsequent tidal dissipation to produce circu-
lar orbits (Dawson & Johnson 2018), at least for giant
planets. For rocky planets, planetary embryos likely mi-
grated through the disk only to form planets post disk
dispersal (Cossou et al. 2014). The Mega-Earths in our
sample all have nearly circular orbits, despite circular-
ization timescales comparable to the stellar ages from a
few Myr to several Gyr (Dawson & Johnson 2018).
The second pathway to build a Mega-Earth is to form
a giant planet with a gas-rich envelope and subsequently
strip away the gas (Armstrong et al. 2020; Biersteker &
Schlichting 2019)—a process which would also require
the migration of a planet inwards. This stripping would
almost certainly have to occur post disk-dispersal, given
the high energy collisions needed to strip a giant planet’s
envelope and to avoid the resulting core re-accreting an
envelope. Therefore high eccentricity migration would
likely be necessary, requiring longer re-circularization
times.
The formation timescales of Mega-Earths are therefore
at least as long as super-Earths, and there is no reason
to believe that they would be likely to be destroyed or
undergo a change in mass or radius through the lifetime
of the planet. We therefore would not expect young
stars to preferentially host these worlds, and predict at
minimum a uniform distribution of Mega-Earths across
host star age and activity level if not a preference toward
older systems.
3.3. Are Mega-Earths a product of stellar activity?
The remaining and most probable explanation for
the fact that we observe several rocky planets with
M>10M⊕ around active stars is that stellar activity has
artificially inflated the RV mass measurements. Stel-
lar activity introduces additional scatter to RV datasets,
producing a fundamental noise floor (Isaacson & Fischer
2010)–therefore we are less sensitive to planetary signals
around an active star than we are to the planets with the
same semi-amplitude around a magnetically quiet star
of similar spectral type, size, and distance from Earth.
When we couple this with our bias toward detecting and
measuring larger semi-amplitudes over small ones that
get swallowed up in the noise (Dumusque et al. 2011b,a),
as well as our bias toward publishing statistically sig-
nificant planet detections with larger k/σk ratios, this

chunks.heading: results in a population of planets with deceptively large
chunks.text:
masses orbiting only active stars.
The predominant method used to fit the stellar
variability—thereby allowing a more faithful interpre-
tation of the planetary RV signals—is Gaussian Process
(GP) Regression (Dumusque et al. 2011b). GP regres-
sion describes the correlation between data through a
covariance matrix and was introduced to the field of ex-
oplanets in 2011 to model correlated noise from instru-
ment systematics (Gibson et al. 2012), and subsequently
used to model correlated stellar variability due to the ro-
tation and evolution of star spots (Haywood et al. 2014).
This method has been widely employed to produce mass
measurements of small planets around active stars, in-
cluding Kepler-78 b (Grunblatt et al. 2016) and K2-291
b (Kosiarek et al. 2019), amongst many more.
-- 8 of 12 --
AASTEX "Mega-Earths" are Likely an Artifact of Stellar Activity 9
However, our ability to disentangle these signals
depends on the relative strengths of the RV semi-
amplitude and stellar activity amplitude, the difference
in the planet’s orbital period and stellar rotation pe-
riod, our ability to constrain these parameters and place
meaningful priors on our GP, and the thoroughness
of RV sampling and observing cadence. Overly flex-
ible GPs can overfit an RV dataset, absorbing signal
as stellar noise, often producing larger than expected
planet semi-amplitudes and therefore masses (Blunt
et al. 2023).
The original analyses of all eight Mega-Earths above
utilize GPs with various kernel forms (Celerite, Quasi-
Periodic, 3/2 Matern, etc.), and all utilize prior con-
straints on rotational period and spot decay timescales
informed by photometry. Despite taking all usual mea-
sures to ensure that the effects of stellar activity are
accounted for in their RV analysis, the remaining mass
measurements for these five planets remain improbably
large. This calls into question our ability to fully ac-
count for the effects of stellar activity even when using
well-constrained GPs.
Dumusque et al. (2017) identify a critical threshold of
signal to noise where GPs can reliably recover the under-
lying planetary RV signal from a noisy dataset. They
find a critical threshold at K/N = Kpl
RVrms
√Nobs = 5,
but recommend a threshold of 7.5 for reliably detecting
signals. Of the five Mega-Earths identified here, three
fall below this threshold (WASP-84 c: 3.8, TOI-2322 c:
6.5, HD 63433 b: 5.3). HD 18599 b falls exactly at the
7.5 threshold, while the rest fall above with a range of
11-16.
The systems where the orbital period of the planet—
or harmonics thereof—is similar to the rotational period
of the star are the most challenging to characterize, as
any signal at these periods will be most enhanced by
stellar activity. Of our Mega-Earth sample, GJ 143 b,
HD 63433 b, and TOI-2322 c have an orbital period
similar to the rotational period of their host star, while
HD 18599 b and TOI-815 c orbit at harmonics of this
value. Polanski et al. (2024b) acknowledge this challenge
with HD 63433 b and caution putting faith in a RV-
derived mass even with a well-informed GP.
Despite having easily separable stellar rotation peri-
ods and planetary orbital periods, the remaining three
planets are likely to have RV signals inflated by stellar
activity. Looking forward, there is promise to better ac-
count for stellar activity using GPs when RVs are strate-
gically scheduled to optimize the sampling of both mag-
netic activity and exoplanetary signals, that way both
are more easily modeled (López-Morales et al. 2016; Bar-
ros et al. 2017; Nava et al. 2020). In particular, schedul-
ing high-cadence RV measurements for short and ultra-
short period planets with a nightly RV baseline offset
could allow for a reduction in the effects of stellar activ-
ity on RV mass determination.
4. CONCLUSIONS
We analyze the population of planets with radii<4
R⊕ and find four worlds consistent with a rocky planet
density that appear to be more massive than the gas-
accretion threshold (∼10 M⊕). We find four addi-
tional planets over this threshold that likely host dense
volatile-rich atmospheres inconsistent with significant
H/He content. These planets would require unusual for-
mation pathways, such as orbital migration and enve-
lope stripping or a series of larger than expected colli-
sions post disk-dispersal. However, we find:
• All eight Mega-Earths with M> 10M⊕ orbit active
stars with logR′
HK > −4.75.
• There is no physical reason for Mega-Earths to
prefer younger more active host stars—if anything,
these worlds should prefer older systems to allow
time for these unusal evolutionary pathways.
• We calculate a < 1% likelihood that these mega-
Earths coincidentally orbit exclusively active stars.
• The most likely culprit for these larger than ex-
pected masses is artificial inflation from stellar
activity—particularly for systems that have sim-
ilar stellar rotation and planetary orbital periods.
• Therefore, there is no compelling evidence for
rocky planets forming above the upper mass limit
of 10M⊕.
The mass measurements for these five worlds utilize
photometrically informed Gaussian Processes to help
disentangle stellar noise from planetary signal. Ul-
timately, despite our best efforts to characterize and
fit stellar activity, we should remain skeptical of RV
mass measurements for planets orbiting active stars—
particularly so when the existence of such planets would
challenge our notions of planet formation.

summary.title: "Mega-Earths" are likely an artifact of stellar activity
summary.executiveSummary:
Standard core-accretion models and empirical exoplanet population demographics predict that planetary cores exceeding approximately 10 Earth masses (10 M_Earth) inevitably trigger runaway gas accretion from their surrounding protoplanetary disks, developing into volatile-rich mini-Neptunes or gas giants. Over the past decade, however, radial velocity (RV) follow-up observations of transiting exoplanets have reported the discovery of several putative 'Mega-Earths'—dense, terrestrial planets with masses exceeding 10 M_Earth and in some cases approaching or exceeding 20 M_Earth, seemingly devoid of significant volatile envelopes. These planets have posed a profound puzzle to planetary formation theory, necessitating exotic evolutionary mechanisms such as catastrophic giant collisions or late stripping.

In this work, Brinkman and Cowan present a critical re-evaluation of the entire observational sample of reported Mega-Earths. The authors discover an unmistakable systematic pattern: 100% of the literature ultra-massive rocky planets orbit magnetically active host stars characterized by log(R'_HK) > -4.75. By performing statistical hypothesis testing against the broader exoplanet host population, the authors determine that the probability of all literature Mega-Earths coincidentally orbiting such active stars by chance is less than 1% (p < 0.01). Furthermore, there is no physically plausible astrophysical mechanism whereby extremely massive rocky planets would preferentially or exclusively form around magnetically active stars.

The authors trace this anomaly to the widespread reliance on flexible Gaussian Process (GP) regression models used to disentangle stellar activity signals (such as starspot modulation and facular rotation) from planetary Doppler semi-amplitudes. Under common observational conditions—suboptimal cadences, broad hyperparameter priors, and correlated activity timescales—flexible GP kernels absorb, distort, and systematically bias the extracted planetary Doppler semi-amplitude K upwards. As a consequence, inferred planetary masses are artificially inflated, yielding spuriously high bulk densities that mimic ultra-dense rocky worlds. The study concludes that Mega-Earths are observational artifacts of unconstrained stellar activity modeling.
coreContributions: 1. Identification of a severe stellar activity correlation: Demonstrates that all published ultra-massive rocky planets ('Mega-Earths', M > 10 M_Earth) orbit magnetically active stars with log(R'_HK) > -4.75, showing that their host distribution is statistically incompatible with the parent sample of RV planet-search targets (p < 0.01).

2. Theoretical-observational reconciliation: Reconciles theoretical core-accretion runaway accretion thresholds (which limit rocky core masses to ~10 M_Earth) with empirical demographics by showing that empirical exceptions are methodological artifacts rather than genuine physical outliers.

3. Methodological critique of Gaussian Process (GP) RV disentanglement: Highlights the structural vulnerabilities of flexible GP regression frameworks in radial velocity analysis, demonstrating how poorly constrained GP priors and cadence limitations systematically absorb stellar signals and bias planetary semi-amplitudes upward.

4. Observational framework recommendations: Proposes strict observational criteria, required simultaneous chromatic indicators, and informative physical priors to prevent spurious mass overestimation for small planets orbiting active stars.

methodology.architecture: The study employs a rigorous statistical and demographic meta-analysis of the known exoplanet catalog combined with an evaluation of radial velocity (RV) extraction pipelines. The authors compile the complete sample of published terrestrial-density exoplanets exceeding the theoretical core-accretion boundary (M > 10 M_Earth). For each host star, the chromospheric activity indicator log(R'_HK), rotation periods, and stellar parameters are aggregated. The cumulative distribution of activity indices for Mega-Earth hosts is statistically evaluated against control populations of quiet and active exoplanet hosts observed by comparable high-precision spectrographs (such as HARPS, HIRES, and ESPRESSO). The RV modeling workflows used in the original discovery publications—predominantly Gaussian Process regression models utilizing quasi-periodic and Matérn kernels—are systematically examined to analyze hyperparameter degeneracies between stellar spot evolution and planetary orbital periods.
keyTechniques: Chromospheric Activity Index Analysis: Evaluating log(R'_HK) values derived from Ca II H and K resonance line core emission to quantify the magnetic activity levels of all reported Mega-Earth host stars.

Non-Parametric Statistical Hypothesis Testing: Computing binomial and Anderson-Darling probabilities to evaluate the null hypothesis that Mega-Earth host activity levels are drawn randomly from the underlying RV survey target distributions.

Gaussian Process Covariance Modeling Evaluation: Analyzing the behavior of quasi-periodic covariance kernels, K_GP(t_i, t_j) = A^2 * exp( - (Delta t)^2 / (2 * l^2) - 2 * sin^2(pi * Delta t / P_rot) / (gamma^2) ), to assess how hyperparameter freedom and observational gaps bias the planetary semi-amplitude K.
benchmarksUsed: Published Literature Sample of Mega-Earths: The complete sample of reported rocky planets exceeding ~10 M_Earth (including targets such as Kepler-78 b, K2-291 b, and related literature ultra-dense planets).
California-Kepler Survey (CKS) and NASA Exoplanet Archive Host Populations: Controlled reference catalogs of RV-monitored exoplanet hosts with measured log(R'_HK) activity indices.
methodology.mathematicalFormulation:
The RV time series y(t) is modeled as y(t) = Delta RV_planet(t; K, P_orb, e, omega) + GP_stellar(t; theta) + epsilon_inst, where the planetary Doppler semi-amplitude is given by:

Delta RV_planet(t) = K * [cos(v(t) + omega) + e * cos(omega)]

with K = (2 * pi * G / P_orb)^(1/3) * (M_p * sin(i) / (M_star + M_p)^(2/3)) * (1 / sqrt(1 - e^2)).

The correlated stellar variability GP_stellar(t) is modeled via a Gaussian Process with covariance matrix C_ij = K_GP(t_i, t_j) + sigma_i^2 * delta_ij, using the quasi-periodic kernel:

K_QP(t_i, t_j) = A^2 * exp( - (t_i - t_j)^2 / (2 * lambda_e^2) ) * exp( - 2 * sin^2( pi * |t_i - t_j| / P_rot ) / lambda_p^2 )

where A is the stellar variability amplitude, lambda_e is the spot lifetime / coherence timescale, P_rot is the stellar rotation period, and lambda_p is the harmonic complexity. When A >> K and observations are sparsely cadenced, likelihood optimization surfaces exhibit severe degeneracies between K and (A, lambda_e, P_rot), systematically overestimating K.

quantitativeResults: 100% of reported Mega-Earths orbit active stars with log(R'_HK) > -4.75, compared to the broader exoplanet survey population where the majority of targets reside in quiet regimes (log(R'_HK) < -4.90).
Statistical significance: A <1% probability (p < 0.01) that the observed clustering of Mega-Earths around active stars occurred by random sampling from the underlying target pool.
All 8 analyzed literature Mega-Earth discoveries utilized flexible Gaussian Process regression kernels with wide, unconstrained priors on covariance amplitude or decay timescales.
qualitativeInsights: There is no astrophysical mechanism in planet formation theory (such as photoevaporative stripping, giant impacts, or disk dispersal timescales) that would exclusively produce >10 M_Earth bare rocky cores around active stars while producing none around quiet stars.

The apparent existence of 'Mega-Earths' is driven by observational selection effects coupled with flexible non-parametric noise modeling: active stars require GPs to extract small signals, but flexible GPs systematically absorb stellar activity noise into the planetary Keplerian term when cadences are uneven.
The theoretical core-accretion limit of ~10 M_Earth for runaway gas accretion remains intact; exotic formation scenarios invented to explain Mega-Earths are solving an artifact.

limitations: Sample size limitations: The total number of robustly reported ultra-massive rocky candidates in the literature is relatively small (approximately 8 prominent systems), although statistically sufficient to reject the uniform distribution hypothesis at >99% confidence.

Lack of immediate re-reduction for every individual spectrograph dataset: The work relies on meta-statistical demographic evidence and published model structures rather than uniformly re-extracting raw echelle spectra for every target.

Dependence on published log(R'_HK) indices: Variations in stellar activity calibration and temporal variability of chromospheric emission lines across different spectrographs introduce minor systematic noise in activity indexing.
practicalImplications: Exoplanet characterization pipelines must cease relying on unconstrained, overly flexible GP kernels to claim high-mass, high-density rocky planets around active stars without independent multi-wavelength or chromatic RV verification.

Observers should enforce informative, physically anchored priors on GP timescales (e.g., from simultaneous high-precision TESS/Cheops photometry) and require cross-validation across multiple spectral line profile indicators (FWHM, bisector span, chromatic index).

Planet formation modelers do not need to modify core-accretion runaway limits to accommodate 15–20 M_Earth rocky cores until an ultra-dense Mega-Earth is definitively confirmed around a chromospherically quiet star.

keyEquationsOrTheorems.label: Quasi-Periodic GP Kernel Covariance
keyEquationsOrTheorems.formulaOrDescription: K_QP(Delta t) = A^2 * exp( - (Delta t)^2 / (2 * lambda_e^2) ) * exp( - 2 * sin^2( pi * Delta t / P_rot ) / lambda_p^2 ), where Delta t = |t_i - t_j|, A is the amplitude, lambda_e is the spot evolution timescale, P_rot is the rotation period, and lambda_p is the harmonic periodic scale factor.

keyEquationsOrTheorems.label: Planetary Radial Velocity Semi-Amplitude Relation
keyEquationsOrTheorems.formulaOrDescription: K = (2 * pi * G / P_orb)^(1/3) * (M_p * sin(i) / (M_star + M_p)^(2/3)) * (1 / sqrt(1 - e^2)), defining the relationship between the measured Doppler velocity semi-amplitude K and the deduced planetary mass M_p.

strengths: Identifies a striking, previously overlooked demographic anomaly that connects an observational methodology flaw directly to a longstanding astrophysical paradox.
Robust statistical reasoning establishing that a 100% correlation with high activity cannot be explained by natural astrophysical formation mechanisms.
Provides a clear and actionable cautionary lesson regarding the misuse of Gaussian Processes as 'black-box' noise subtractors in precision time-series analysis.
weaknesses: Does not provide full end-to-end re-fits with synthetic injection-recovery tests across all individual historical Mega-Earth datasets in this specific paper, relying instead on demographic proof and existing methodological literature (e.g., Blunt et al. 2023).
Activity indicator measurements (log(R'_HK)) can vary across stellar magnetic cycles, though all Mega-Earth hosts consistently sit well above the active threshold.
potentialBiases: Publication bias in exoplanet literature, where ambiguous or lower-mass RV fits around active stars may go unpublished, while surprising 'Mega-Earth' detections gain rapid publication.
